description.narrative:
Norwegian Refugee Council - Norska flyktingrådet (NRC) - har ansökt om ett förnyat partnerskap med Sida 2021-2025.
2021 NRC har dessutom ansökt om finansiering på 364,5 miljoner SEK för att genomföra humanitära insatser i 26 humanitära krisområden under 2021: Afghanistan, Kamerun, Centralafrikanska republiken, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Demokratiska Republiken Kongo, Eritrea, Etiopien, Iran, Irak, Jordanien, Kenya, Libanon, Libyen, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Honduras, El Salvador, Mexiko, Palestina, Somalia, Sydsudan, Sudan, Tanzania / Burundi, Uganda, Venezuela och Jemen. Ansökan inkluderar även 40 miljoner kronor för den humanitära snabbmekanismen (RRM) och 20 miljoner kronor i stöd till sju projekt för metodstöd, kapacitetsuppbyggnad och samordning.
Den aktuella budgeten för NRC:s hela humanitära program 2021 uppgår till 4 263 200 000 NOK, varav Sidas del för närvarande utgör ca 8%. Sida ger NRC möjligheten att nyttja resurser flexibelt inom varje enskilt landprogram, (enligt så kallad Programme-Based Approach – PBA)
Humanitär-Utveckling-Fred Nexus NRC bidrar i hög grad till arbetet för att sammankoppla humanitärt bistånd med freds- och utvecklingsinsatser. Organisationens strävan att effektivisera biståndet genom katalytiskt stöd till samordning och kapacitetsbyggande insatser bidrar till denna ansats. I samarbetet med andra organisationer möjliggör och bidrar NRC:s verksamhet och påverkansarbete till att stärka hållbara lösningar för flyktingar och människor som har blivit tvångsfördrivna och bidrar därmed till att på sikt minska de humanitära behoven. Även krisdrabbade människors möjligheter till självförsörjning prioriteras. NRC:s analyskapacitet är en styrka som bidrar till att programmeringen anpassas till en nexus-ansats och den analys som genomförs av NRC:s internationella center för övervakning av tvångsförflyttning (IDMC) är av stor vikt för dessa analyser. 19 av de 26 kriser i NRC:s portfölj som Sida finansierar avser länder där Sverige även bedriver utvecklingssamarbete vilket öppnar för möjligheter till synergier med humanitärt bistånd.
2022 NRC ska få totalt 455,5 miljoner kronor av Sidas humanitära finansiering, enligt följande fördelning:
- Sida kommer att stödja NRC:s humanitära program i 23 krissituationer som Sida har prioriterat genom sin behovsbaserade allokeringsmodell för 2022, med 288,5 miljoner kronor :Afghanistan, Centralafrikanska republiken, Colombia och regionen (Ecuador, Panamà), Demokratiska republiken Kongo, Etiopien, Irak, Jemen, Jordanien, Kamerun, Kenya, Libanon, Libyen, Mali, Moçambique, Niger, Nigeria, Palestina, Somalia, Sudan, Sydsudan, Syrien, Uganda, Venezuela.
- Flerårig finansiering för NRC :s humanitära program i Demokratiska republiken Kongo, Mali och Nigeria inleds 2022 och Sida har för ändamålet att ta i anspråk 104 miljoner kronor från kommande års anslag från erhållen Bemyndiganderam förutsatt att Riksdagen anvisar tillräckliga medel.
- NRC:s akuta insatser vid plötsligt uppkomna kriser kommer att stödjas genom Sidas snabbinsatsmekanism (RRM) under 2022 med 50 miljoner kronor.
- NRC:s metod- och kapacitetsstärkande projekt för skydd, miljö och IDMC (Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre) kommer under 2022 att få 13 miljoner kronor, varav 3 miljoner kronor från Sida/Globen för IDMC.
Sidas bidrag till NRC för 2022 kommer att täcka cirka 6,5 % av NRC:s totala finansiella behov för de stödda programmen och projekten. Det kommer att tillhandahålla humanitära tjänster till nästan 9 miljoner människor (53 % kvinnor) i Afghanistan, Kamerun, Centralafrikanska republiken, Colombia och regionen, Demokratiska republiken Kongo, Etiopien, Irak, Jordanien, Kenya, Libanon, Libyen, Mali, Moçambique, Niger, Nigeria, Palestina, Somalia, Sydsudan, Sudan, Syrien, Uganda, Venezuela och Jemen.
HUM lägger till 50 MSEK för NRC:s landprogram 2022 i Ukraina som gynnar 90,000 människor med skydd, tak över huvudet, WaSH samt kontantbistånd. Beslut 5 April. Avtalförändring nr 5.
HUM lägger till 7,5 MSEK för NRC:s landprogram 2022 i Kamerun från halvsårsanslaget 2022 (livsmedelsförsörjning, juridik rådgivning för 600 husshållen/4200 individer i Logone-et-Chari, Mayo Sava och Mayo Tsanaga). Beslut 9 juni 2022. Avtalförändring nr 6.
HUM lägger till 10 MSEK för NRC:s landprogram 2022 i Sydsudan från slutsåranslaget. Beslut 16 november 2022, 2022-002341. Avtalförändring nr 7.
2023 NRC ska få totalt 659.5 miljoner kronor (2023-2025) av Sidas humanitära finansiering för att genomföra: - humanitära insatser i 23 krisområden under 2023: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Burkina Faso, Centralafrikanska republiken, Colombia, Demokratiska republiken Kongo, Etiopien, Irak, Jemen, Jordanien, Kamerun, Kenya, Libanon, Mali, Moçambique, Niger, Palestina, Sudan, Sydsudan, Syrien, Uganda, Ukraina och Venezuela. NRC har dessutom ansökt om 244 miljoner kronor för att kunna fortsätta sina humanitära program i Jemen, Kamerun, Sydsudan, Syria och Venezuela under 2024 och 2025. - ansökan inkluderar även 50 miljoner kronor till den humanitära snabbinsatsmekanismen (RRM) - och 40 miljoner kronor i stöd till fyra fleråriga projekt för metodstöd och kapacitetsuppbyggnad: Miljö, Skydd, Tillträde, IDMC (18,5 under 2023, 21,5 under 2024-2025).

The Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) has applied for a renewed strategic partnership with Sida during 2021-2025.
NRC has applied as well to Sida for funding of 364.5 million SEK to carry out “the Humanitarian Programme for 2021” in 26 humanitarian crisis settings: Afghanistan, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Iran, Iraq, Jordan, Kenya, Lebanon, Libya, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Honduras, El Salvador, Mexico, Palestine, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Tanzania/Burundi, Uganda, Venezuela, Yemen. The application includes provision of 40 million SEK to replenish the Rapid Response Mechanism funding instrument and 7 individual projects for method, capacity-building and coordination.
The intervention’s tentative total budget is 4 263 200 000 Norwegian krona (NOK), that the organisation is financing with Sida’s funding in a proportion of 8% approximately. Other donors, like the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, DG ECHO, UNHCR, etc. are the largest contributors, besides a dozen of other donors in agreement with NRC. Sida provides NRC with the opportunity to allocate resources flexibly within individual country programmes (Programme-Based Approach – PBA). ¬ NRC's catalytic support for coordination and capacity building contributes greatly to the link between humanitarian aid, development and peace. NRC's advocacy work and activities enable, at least contribute to, sustainable solutions for refugees and displaced people in a significant way in cooperation with other actors. In the long run, the NRC will reduce humanitarian needs. The NRC prioritizes self-sufficiency in its programs. The NRC's analysis capability, not least through its Internal Displacement Monitoring Center (IDMC), is an advantage for relevant programming according to the nexus orientations. Among the 26 crises in NRC's portfolio that Sida prioritizes, there are 15 where Sida implements Sweden's development strategies in synergy with humanitarian aid.
In 2022 support NRC with 455,5 MSEK in total of Sida’s humanitarian funding, according to the following breakdown: - The grant will support NRC humanitarian programmes in 23 crises settings that Sida has prioritized through its needs-based allocation model, with 288.5 MSEK during 2022: Afghanistan, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Colombia and region, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Ethiopia, Iraq, Jordan, Kenya, Lebanon, Libya, Mali, Mozambique, Niger, Nigeria, Palestine, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Syria, Uganda, Venezuela, Yemen - As multi-annual funding for emergency response in DR Congo, Mali and Nigeria is initiated in 2022, the grant will provide as well NRC with outstanding financial commitments from Sida, estimated 104 MSEK for 2023-2024. - NRC emergency response in sudden onset crises will be supported through Sida’s Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) window with 50 MSEK for 2022. - NRC’s method and capacity development projects for Protection, Environment and the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) will receive 13 MSEK, including 3 MSEK from Sida/Globen for IDMC. Sida’s contribution to NRC for 2022 will cover around 6.5% of NRC’s total financial requirements of the supported programmes and projects. It will provides humanitarian services to almost 9 million persons (53% female). HUM adds 50 MSEK for NRC's 2022 country programme in Ukraine benefiting 90,000 people with protection, shelter, WaSH and cash assistance. Decision 5 April. Amendment nr. 5. HUM adds 7.5 MSEK for NRC's 2022 country programme in Cameroon from the 2022 mid-year allocation (food security, legal advice for 600 households/4200 individuals in Logone-et-Chari, Mayo Sava and Mayo Tsanaga). Decision 9 June 2022. Contract amendment No 6. HUM adds 10 MSEK for NRC's 2022 country programme in South Sudan from the end-of-the-year allocation. Decision 16 November 2022 nr 2022-002341. Contract amendment No 7.
2023 NRC will receive a total of SEK 659.5 million (2023-2025) of Sida's humanitarian funding to implement: - humanitarian operations in 23 crisis areas in 2023: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Burkina Faso, Central African Republic, Colombia, Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, Iraq, Yemen, Jordan, Cameroon, Kenya, Lebanon, Mali, Mozambique, Niger, Palestine, Sudan, South Sudan, Syria, Uganda, Ukraine and Venezuela. NRC has also applied for SEK 244 million to continue its humanitarian programmes in Yemen, Cameroon, South Sudan, Syria and Venezuela in 2024 and 2025. - The application also includes SEK 50 million for the Rapid Reaction Mechanism (RRM) - and SEK 40 million in support of four multi-year projects for methodological support and capacity building: Environment, Protection, Access, IDMC (18.5 MSEKin 2023, 21.5 MSEK in 2024-2025). Decision dated ... March 2023. Contract amendment No 8.
NRC targets 7.7 million unique beneficiaries in total within Sida-funded humanitarian programmes in 2023, (52% female), who will receive protection and humanitarian services from NRC: Education, WASH, Shelter and settlement, Food security and livelihoods, including multi-purpose cash assistance, Protection, Legal assistance, Humanitarian mediation (community-based peace-building). Advocacy and support to humanitarian coordination and durable solution to displacements working groups in the field are part of NRC's engagement that Sida is funding. NRC's annual budget 2023 in the settings and thematics prioritized by Sida amounts to 5620 million Norwegian crowns in total. Sida's share weighs so far 8% of it: NRC's third largest donor whose cumulated 2021-2025 grant is 80% softly earmarked (programme-based approach) and 34% multi-year.
Earlier granted multi-year funding for 2023 was disbursed in January (52 MSEK) in support to continued humanitarian operations in DR Congo, Mali and Nigeria with strong emphasis on emergency response.

Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) is Norway's largest international humanitarian organisation and widely recognized as a leading field-based displacement agency within the international humanitarian community. NRC is the INGO receiving the largest contribution from Sida's Humanitarian Unit to INGOs so far, based on experience of successful partnerships, NRC's capacities to respond at scale and its coverage of crises that Sida is prioritizing through the needs-based allocation approach. NRC receives approximately 8% of Sida's humanitarian unit's annual budget appropriation.
The objectives of NRC can be summarized as follows: "To protect the rights of displaced and vulnerable people during crisis, to provide assistance meeting their immediate humanitarian needs, to prevent further displacement and to contribute to durable solutions, and to provide expertise as a strategic partner to humanitarian systems and actors." NRCs main activity is delivery of humanitarian assistance through programme activities in the field. NRC specializes in six areas of expertise, or "core competencies": shelter and settlements; livelihoods and food security; information, counselling and legal assistance (ICLA); education; camp management; and water, sanitation and hygiene promotion (WASH). Protection is lifted up as a new core competency of NRC since 2021. NRC engages closely with the affected populations to understand their needs and capacities, ensuring it tailors its assistance accordingly and involve them in the entire programme cycle, from design through implementation to evaluation. NRC advocates for respect for the rights of displaced and vulnerable people.
In 2021, the NRC Board approved the Global Strategy 20222025. The strategy sets out four sub-objectives for areas that NRC will continue to strengthen and further institutionalize, namely, 1. assistance to hard-to-reach populations, 2. humanitarian policy, 3. protection, and 4. durable solutions. It also points to four areas of work that will be accelerated through expanded engagement and investments: i) advocacy, ii) climate and environment, iii) collaboration with local actors, and iv) quality programming.
NRCs work is divided into three pillars: humanitarian assistance, advocacy and expert deployment. Sida's Humanitarian Unit funding will continue prioritizing mainly the first pillar through funding of the humanitarian country programmes in line with HRPs and the RRPs and through the RRM funding. To some extent, Sida will support as well the second pillar of advocacy which is integrated in the humanitarian country programmes and implemented by NRC's method, thematic and capacity development projects supported by Sida. Sida will provide NRC with only a punctual support to the third pillar, through funding to CashCap which is deploying experts to the field for invigorating cash assistance working groups (17 in 2020 to 16 countries).
The Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) has applied for a renewed strategic partnership with Sida during 2021-2025.
NRC has applied as well to Sida for funding of 364.5 million SEK to carry out the Humanitarian Programme for 2021 in 26 humanitarian crisis settings: Afghanistan, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Iran, Iraq, Jordan, Kenya, Lebanon, Libya, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Honduras, El Salvador, Mexico, Palestine, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Tanzania/Burundi, Uganda, Venezuela, Yemen. The application includes provision of 40 million SEK to replenish the Rapid Response Mechanism funding instrument and 7 individual projects for method, capacity-building and coordination.
The interventions tentative total budget is 4 263 200 000 Norwegian krona (NOK), that the organisation is financing with Sidas funding in a proportion of 8% approximately. Other donors, like the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, DG ECHO, UNHCR, etc. are the largest contributors, besides a dozen of other donors in agreement with NRC. Sida provides NRC with the opportunity to allocate resources flexibly within individual country programmes (Programme-Based Approach PBA).
NRC's catalytic support for coordination and capacity building contributes greatly to the link between humanitarian aid, development and peace. NRC's advocacy work and activities enable, at least contribute to, sustainable solutions for refugees and displaced people in a significant way in cooperation with other actors. In the long run, the NRC will reduce humanitarian needs. The NRC prioritizes self-sufficiency in its programs. The NRC's analysis capability, not least through its Internal Displacement Monitoring Center (IDMC), is an advantage for relevant programming according to the nexus orientations. Among the 26 crises in NRC's portfolio that Sida prioritizes, there are 15 where Sida implements Sweden's development strategies in synergy with humanitarian aid.
In 2022 support NRC with 455.5 MSEK in total of Sidas humanitarian funding, according to the following breakdown: - The grant will support NRC humanitarian programmes in 23 crises settings that Sida has prioritized through its needs-based allocation model, with 288.5 MSEK during 2022. - As multi-annual funding for emergency response in DR Congo, Mali and Nigeria is initiated in 2022, the grant will provide as well NRC with outstanding financial commitments from Sida, estimated 104 MSEK for 2023-2024. - NRC emergency response in sudden onset crises will be supported through Sidas Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) window with 50 MSEK for 2022. - NRCs method and capacity development projects for Protection, Environment and the Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) will receive 13 MSEK, including 3 MSEK from Sida/Globen for IDMC. Sidas contribution to NRC for 2022 will cover around 6.5% of NRCs total financial requirements of the supported programmes and projects. It will provides humanitarian services to almost 9 million persons (53% female). HUM adds 50 MSEK for NRC's 2022 country programme in Ukraine benefiting 90,000 people with protection, shelter, WaSH and cash assistance. Decision 5 April. Amendment nr. 5. HUM adds 7.5 MSEK for NRC's 2022 country programme in Cameroon from the 2022 mid-year allocation (food security, legal advice for 600 households/4200 individuals in Logone-et-Chari, Mayo Sava and Mayo Tsanaga). Decision 9 June 2022. Contract amendment No 6.
From Conclusion on performances September 2022:
NRC foresees that 8,986,125 persons (53.4% female) will benefit from NRC's humanitarian services in 2022 in 35 crisis settings. It is however likely that NRC will over-achieve again its initial target.
NRC is on a continued trajectory of growth in the delivery of cash and vouchers to people affected by displacement. The trend should be brought at scale, given the multiplying effect on empowered beneficiaries. Impacts of Multi-purpose cash assistance could be researched and highlighted further by NRC for promoting cash assistance as the best option, becoming hopefully the default method for the provision of humanitarian assistance everywhere and for all actors.
Education was a declining sector for NRC in 2020 and 2021 due to closure of schools under Covid-19. It generated many new protection risks, like early marriage for girls, early pregnancies, drop-out of school-aged children from education, and psychosocial needs. Restart of education services is going on in 2022. Meanwhile, following the pandemic, NRC saw the rapid scale up of psychosocial support programme, the Better Learning Programme (BLP). Building on lessons learned from the Middle East region, it has rolled-out BLP to both Central and West Africa (CWA) and Latin America. To reach children stuck at home, NRC developed a BLP smartphone application for both parents and teachers.
Protection
NRC developed Minimum Standards on Safe and Inclusive Programming (protection mainstreaming) which are now incorporated into the Global Strategy (2022-2025) as a critical component of programme quality. Mainstreamed and integrated protection are generating increasingly protection outcomes within NRC's humanitarian assistance.
Protection is evolving into a full new core competence of NRC as from 2022 with stand-alone protection capacities and interventions wherever relevant.
NRC has been essential in hosting the Sida-funded IASC protection policy review in 2021.
Information, Counselling and Legal Assistance (ICLA) in particular for Housing, Land and Property issues (HLP) remain the domain of excellence of NRC that only few other protection actors can match and replace. Solved documentation problems related to legal identity, civil status and property is key to the protection of the displaced people, including children and women.
Inclusive programming
NRC reports a systematic engagement with communities in term of participation to the design and orientation of the response.
Its ambition to shift resolutely towards increased equal to equal partnerships, especially to mobilize local resources among the civil society, was not yet articulated in 2021 in term of localized partnerships and will be hopefully worked through during the strategic cycle 2022-2025. NRC has a long way to go, as its is mainly implementing interventions by itself.
Sida's helpdesk on gender had reservation about NRC's effective gender mainstreaming in programming and reporting. The outcome is certainly better, in most cases, than reported. NRC has to ensure that it captures this dimension in its programme documents (both applications and reports).
Data security and protection risk management do not give visibility to the assistance and the protection services delivered by NRC to LGBTQI people. Sida should respect this and not request specific dis-aggregated data capturing this beneficiary groups. Sida has evidence that NRC protection work is non-discriminatory and reaches out effectively people with specific needs, including LGBTQI people.
Coordination
NRC is a key asset of the global and local humanitarian systems for its dedicated participation to coordination forums, bringing to them its principled approach and expertise for humanitarian action: the IASC, humanitarian country teams, advisory groups, clusters, hosted and facilitated NGO forums, working groups in many areas and sectors, including durable solutions to displacements. It is not infrequent that NRC co-leads protection, shelter, food security, education, camp management clusters. Such constructive participation is making a difference and is likely to improve the humanitarian system.
Advocacy 2021
NRC continued its advocacy work on Sanctions and Counter-terrorism measures affecting humanitarian service delivery, in particular in Afghanistan.
NRC released its flagship annual report on the Worlds Most Neglected Displacement Crises, which analyses displacement crises based on lack of funding, lack of media attention, and lack of international political and diplomatic initiatives.
NRC's Secretary General became the Eminent Person of the Grand Bargain. Through this role, NRC is in a unique position to steer reforms aimed at improving the system, through efforts such as ensuring that implementing organisations receive a critical mass of quality funding and working towards making the aid system more localized.
NRC's Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC), co-funded by HUM and INTEM at Sida, launched its 2021 Global Report on Internal Displacement (GRID), featuring a special focus on disaster displacement and the impacts of climate change, exploring the intersections of climate, disasters, and internal displacement.
Most country offices are producing frequent advocacy documents about the rights of displaced populations, voiceless affected communities and humanitarian contexts that are highly appreciated and of good quality.
Humanitarian policy-making 2021
As part of NRCs Global Strategy process, a Climate and Environment Strategy 2030 was developed, focusing on strengthening NRCs response in the areas of climate adaptation, access to clean energy, and reduced environmental footprint. NRC also signed the Climate and Environment Charter for Humanitarian Organisations, which entails a commitment to work on climate adaptation and mitigation, including through setting public time-bound targets for emissions reductions. NRC also initiated work to establish environmental minimum standards for its programmes. These were developed for shelter and settlements, WASH, livelihood and food security, and emergency response.
Nexus
NRC has drawn lessons from pilot experience of 'humanitarian mediation' in Mali, DRC and CAR during 2017-2020 that was funded by Sida/FRED (#11611). The external final evaluation concluded that this pilot phase of introducing peace-building within the scope of NRC's programmes would deserve to be followed by another pilot experience correcting the shortcomings of the initiative that was found not fully relevant, efficient and successful. The lack of capacities in implementing the new programme in three very challenging contexts was pointed out. It does not mean that NRC should abandon the idea to try again. Preventing protection risks, including those resulting to forced displacements, by mitigating tensions and antagonism between communities, is highly needed in crisis contexts. But it requires an expertise and partnerships that cannot be built overnight. NRC should be encouraged to persist.
NRC is better placed for linking emergency and recovery when it explores and supports durable solutions to displacement. The development leg of the nexus falls within NRC's natural mandate, although it cannot or should not be resourced by Sida's humanitarian funding, but rather by development budget-lines. NRC is meant to support IDPs and refugees before, during and after displacements and to accompany them until displacements cease to affect them, because they could be repatriated, resettled or locally integrated in a sustainable and dignified way. It is unclear whether durable solutions interventions of NRC are budgeted within NRC's country humanitarian programmes that are submitted to Sida or resourced within longer-term strategies. It is not unusual that Sida colleagues visiting NRC in the field give as a feedback that NRC's interventions are getting near development work, because the response is protracted and because it addresses rather recovery needs than life-saving needs. HUM is however very clear to NRC in its dialogue by highlighting that HUM funding is for humanitarian interventions only and within the frameworks of OCHA's and UNHCR's humanitarian appeals, if they exist. It is however often difficult, if one should ever do it, to draw a clear and separate line between humanitarian action and recovery/resilience/durable solutions. In some countries, especially in protracted refugee / displacement situations that are no more acute crises, support to care and maintenance, to self-reliance and to durable solutions, like in Jordan for instance, represents the bulk of NRC's programme, while emergency life-saving and protection services are less necessary. Such interventions would be better supported by longer-term development or recovery budget-lines, within the framework of the Global Compact for Refugees and the Comprehensive Refugee Response Framework. Development donors are increasingly getting involved, including Sida, but too slow, too late and too short. Meanwhile, assisting aid-dependent IDPs and refugees throughout the years / decades of their displacement career, like the Palestinan refugees and many other caseloads, remains resourced mainly by humanitarian budget-lines, including Sida's.
Sida's assessment on performance and results
Alike many other actors in the sector, NRC excels in reporting activities and outputs, but should be better in catching what changes and impacts its interventions have resulted to ultimately on assisted communities. The reporting of data and results does not provide necessarily an accurate and consolidated overview of what NRC has achieved. Sida has notified NRC that it should provide dis-aggregated data by age in targeting and reporting which is a norm.
NRC has still a long way to go for building programme partnerships and localizing its programmes. NRC channeled Sida funding in 2021 to only 15 partners in total, including 4 INGOs, for a very little proportion of the total humanitarian funding received from Sida, below 1%, less than in 2019 and 2020 (3%). NRC is however party to many consortia and excels in cooperating with local authorities and actors, and building their capacitries, although not through financial transactions.
Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM)
HUM granted 40 MSEK to NRC in 2021 as the annual RRM allocation amount, without replenishment during the course of the year, as in 2019. NRC managed to utilize this emergency response funding window sparingly until October 2021, supporting 14 projects in 13 countries. In 2022, the allocation amounted to 50 MSEK; this funding allocation is almost completely exhausted (4 MSEK left), after support to 12 projects in 12 countries has been approved.

description.narrative:
Programmes and projects results 2021
In 2021, NRC targeted close to 7.3 million beneficiaries in its Final submission and reported that it reached out ultimately 9.8 million people in need in 35 countries during that year. This is 25% over planned results. This is due to several factors: first, contexts where NRC has intervened have been facing increased humanitarian needs while NRC's initial and contingency planning scenarios were conservative, Covid-19's primary and secondary impacts continued to affect people in crisis settings, then, NRC's comparative advantages have generated increased funding opportunities augmenting out-reach and outcomes.
Considering that HUM provided NRC with 7.9% of its total received humanitarian funding in 2021 from over 20 donors, it could be counted that HUM supported the full NRC humanitarian services for 775,000 persons.
NRC comes first as NGO in 2021 in term of level of received funding tracked by OCHA with a 4.7% share of total humanitarian funding globally (FTS). NRC continues to occupy a niche as a top humanitarian actor in its category. It has just been awarded the Conrad Hilton Foundation's Humanitarian Prize (US$ 2.5 million) in 2022, "judged to have made extraordinary contributions toward alleviating human suffering".
Lifting up just a few examples of NRC's achievements in 2021, Sida will remember that
- NRC is reporting having distributed 97,2 million USD in cash and voucher assistance in 2021 a 25% increase compared to 2020, almost entirely due to the increase in the distribution of multi-purpose cash;
- In 2021, NRC developed Minimum Standards on Safe and Inclusive Programming (Protection) which are now incorporated into the Global Strategy (2022-2025) as a critical component of programme quality;
- NRC initiated work to establish environmental minimum standards for its programmes. These were developed for shelter and settlements, WASH, livelihood and food security, and emergency response. Sida follows closing how NRC is 'greening' its programmes.
- Following the pandemic, NRC saw the rapid scale up of its flagship psychosocial support programme, the Better Learning Programme (BLP). To reach children stuck at home, NRC developed a BLP smartphone application for both parents and teachers.
- In 2021, 37 cases concerning SEA were opened and investigated by NRC, across all funding donors, approximately 20% were referred to authorities or to other organisations for appropriate follow up and support; and on 30 June, as each year since 2013, NRC published on its website information about the anti-corruption work related to the previous year: a total of 92 cases of alleged financial corruption/misconduct were investigated in 2020. 56 cases were found to be either groundless, not substantiated or related to negligence and bad performance. 5 cases were avoided due to early detection, and 7 cases are pending conclusion.
- In Afghanistan, NRC provided certified seeds, agriculture tools to the farmers and supported local products to expand their businesses along with focusing on livestock and smart climate agriculture programming in rural areas of Afghanistan.
- In Cameroon, NRC facilitated the establishment of 6,535 birth certificates (44% girls) through declaratory judgements. Radio broadcasts in different local languages informed communities about the importance of birth certificates and the process to obtain them.
- In CAR, , NRC reached 60,399 people with WASH interventions, including 27,934 men and 32,465 women, representing an increase in 32% over last year.
- NRCs protection teams in Colombia, Ecuador and Panama carried out information and training sessions with targeted communities and local authorities on protection issues including violence prevention and risk mitigation, while designing and developing local protection strategies with the participation of leaders, communities and local authorities.
- Targeted legal assistance helped reduce the risk of child statelessness in Beni, DRC.
... Every country programmes offer interesting results to highlight.
2021 achieved results and 2022 planned targets are below 2020 results (12 million people assisted) achieved by NRC by 18% and 26% respectively. 2020 saw a huge investment of NRC in WASH and awareness-raising related activities to address COVID-19 and lockdown impacts; this explains the steep increase in beneficiary numbers for that year. Although, WASH continued to be the main sector of NRC's humanitarian services in 2021 due to Covid-19 (46% of its beneficiaries receiving WASH services), NRC in 2021 (and in 2022) is facing the challenges of reduced funding globally and of continued access challenges. However, 2021 beneficiary numbers are still 7% higher than for 2019 the pre-pandemic year (9.1 million). NRC is therefore continuing upwards on the gradual curve of beneficiary reach out despite obstacles.

title.narrative: Provision of integrated health and nutrition life-saving services to famine affected and displaced population in Central Unity, Upper Nile and Greater Equatoria regions

description.narrative: The objective of this joint WHO/UNICEF/UNFPA/IOM health project is to provide much needed life-saving services (emergency health and nutrition services) to displaced populations and host communities affected by food insecurity, including famine, and violence in Greater Equatoria (Kajo-Keji, Lainya, Magwi, Torit and Yei), Unity (Koch, Mayendit, Leer and Panyijar), and in Upper Nile (Fashoda- Aburoc). The CERF grant will be used to mount the initial response to provide life-saving primary healthcare services to 135,000 people. In particular, UNICEF will procure and deliver 250,000 measles vaccines and vaccine consumables and procure supplies for and maintain emergency cold chain systems.

title.narrative: South Sudan - Emergency Water, Sanitation and Health - World Vision Canada 2014
Soudan du Sud - Aide d'urgence en eau, assainissement et santé - Vision Mondiale Canada 2014

description.narrative: March 2014 - The complex humanitarian situation in South Sudan has become worse since fighting broke out between government and anti-government forces in December 2013. The fighting has displaced some 710,000 people within South Sudan, and more than 170,000 people have sought protection in neighbouring countries. Agricultural production is disrupted, and essential basic services, such as safe drinking water, schools, and medical facilities have been shut down or destroyed in the fighting. Humanitarian needs include food, health care, shelter, protection services, water, sanitation and hygiene. With DFATD’s support, World Vision Canada is providing emergency water, sanitation and supplemental feeding to 63,360 conflict-affected and food-insecure people in Warrap State, South Sudan. Project activities include: (1) establishing nine new water points in seven health facilities and rehabilitating 15 boreholes for 12,400 people; (2) establishing 24 water committees to manage, operate and maintain new water points and constructing 6 blocks of latrines in four communities, benefitting over 900 people; (3) training five community hygiene promoters and conducting five sanitation and hygiene training sessions; and (4) providing supplemental feeding to 9,484 children under-five and 1,897 malnourished pregnant or lactating women.

Mars 2014 – La situation humanitaire complexe au Soudan du Sud s’est grandement détériorée depuis que des violences ont éclaté, en décembre 2013, entre le gouvernement et les forces qui lui sont opposées. La situation a forcé quelque 710 000 personnes à se déplacer à l’intérieur du Soudan du Sud, et plus de 170 000 Sud-Soudanais ont cherché refuge dans des pays voisins. La production agricole a cessé et les infrastructures de services essentiels, tels que le réseau d’approvisionnement en eau potable, les écoles et les installations médicales, ont été fermées ou détruites en raison des violences. Parmi les besoins humanitaires recensés en 2014, notons les aliments, les soins de santé, les abris, les services de protection, l’eau, l’assainissement et l’hygiène. Avec le soutien du MAECD, Vision Mondiale Canada offre des services d’approvisionnement en eau, d’assainissement et de suppléments alimentaires d’urgence à 63 360 personnes touchées par le conflit ou l’insécurité alimentaire dans l’État de Warrap (Soudan du Sud). Parmi les activités de ce projet : 1) établir neuf nouveaux points d’eau dans sept installations sanitaires et remettre en état 15 puits au profit de 12 400 personnes; 2) établir 24 comités de gestion de l’eau qui géreront, opéreront et entretiendront de nouveaux points d’eau et construire six blocs de latrines dans quatre collectivités, au profit de plus de 900 personnes; 3) former cinq promoteurs de l’hygiène communautaire et mener cinq séances de formation sur l’assainissement et l’hygiène; 4) offrir des suppléments alimentaires à 9 484 enfants de moins de cinq ans et à 1 897 femmes enceintes ou allaitantes qui sont dénutries.

title.narrative: Emergency response to acute and chronic complex health emergencies and increased access to health care for vulnerable populations in South Sudan

description.narrative:
Through this project Medair will respond to prioritised, assessed, unmet health needs or gaps in primary health service provision, to reduce morbidity and mortality of vulnerable girls, boys, women and men in conflict affected and other vulnerable states.
This project aims to improve access to quality preventative and curative primary health care services, including reproductive health. Due to the underlying vulnerabilities of the population, high maternal and under 5 mortality rates, this project will focus on improving access of quality life-saving services to pregnant and lactating women and children under 5 years. This project will maintain provision of essential primary health care services to IDPs and the host community in Renk County where the health system has been dysfunctional as a result of the conflict. The project will also maintain Medair’s health mobile response capacity to act as “First Responders” in an emergency location following a needs assessment, as well as to scale-up this first response in the absence of other partners. Medair’s health emergency response team forms part of a well-established multi-sector emergency response team that has been responding to acute emergencies across South Sudan for more than 10 years. Medair deploys health personnel and life-saving assistance at short notice, to assess or respond to needs triggered by acute health emergencies in the country. Medair's mobile teams propose to respond to the needs of communities affected by outbreak of disease or other public health emergencies and to communities displaced or impacted by the ongoing conflict.
This project also aims to support the Ministry of Health and other relevant authorities in emergency response capacity, training local male and female health workers to respond to health emergencies and providing training in disease surveillance, outbreak response, case management, reporting systems, and awareness of various health gender needs based on current disease trends.

title.narrative: Emergency Shelter and NFI support to the displaced people living in hard to reach areas.

description.narrative: The project aims to provide Survival Kits /Emergency shelter/ NFIs both in-kind and in Cash modalities to the most vulnerable people specifically the unexpectedly new displaced, newly returnees, and some host communities. This is a proposed 6 months project starting from 1st March 2019 focusing on the distribution of SK/Shelter/NFI kits using rapid response mechanism (mobile Teams) to reach out 9100 beneficiaries in Unity state. The proposed counties within the selected state are Panyijiar, Mayendit, and Rubkona. The project will promote timely delivery of assistance through deployment of mobile teams in line with humanitarian priorities for 2019 as outlined in the HRP as well as the nature of the emergency in South Sudan. NRC’s mobile response teams will be ready for deployment within 8 days to conduct assessments and within 14 days for full-fledged delivery of NFIs and emergency shelters either in-kind or Cash depending on the location. The project team will work in close coordination with S/NFI cluster and its activities will be informed by the gaps identified through the assessment missions in which NRC will participate and/or carry out alone depending on the situation between Mar 2019 and Aug 2019. NRC was involved in AAP since 2018 through the Shelter cluster, where trainings on AAP, Communication and Community Engagement was conducted in Ibba county, in Dec, 2018. Currently NRC is one of two focal points for AAP in Shelter cluster, and is involved in Communication and Community Engagement working group. Lately NRC delivered a presentation on AAP in the Shelter cluster meeting for all partners to introduce them more on what have been done and the way forward. Building on this, NRC will be conducting AAP as first step before the assessment or the intervention phase, and will ensure the diversity during training, to make sure that the community and the local authority are fully aware with all details, including their roles and responsibilities. The project team will work on raising the community and local authority’s engagements and it will empower them to cope with the faced challenges. Using the AAP approach, NRC will adapt the project to the specific needs of men, women, girls and boys and respond accordingly or refer to relevant service providers in case the needs cannot be covered by the response. NRC use its check list of protection mainstreaming to complement the multi sector assessment. The distribution of life-saving Shelter and NFI kits or Cash, will be done in distribution sites which will be identified together with the community and will put into consideration the minimum standards of protection. Since NRC is also working in WASH, Food security and education sectors therefore a synergy will be sought when responding to the shelter/NFI needs. The project team will ensure that women and girls are not exposed to risk of sex and gender based violence (SGBV) at the distribution points and within short walking distances from the beneficiaries’ homes. In case drinking water is not available in nearby locations, water will be provided by the NRC team at the distribution sites. Elderly, physically incapable, pregnant women and others who require special attention will be prioritized during distribution so that they are served early and comfortably. Feedback desk will be provided at each distribution site so that beneficiaries register their complaints with NRC on the entire project process and quality of the supplies/Kits. NRC will complement its distribution by community awareness campaign and information sessions. NRC will conduct post distribution Monitoring (PDM) in at least at 50% in locations of distribution. NRC will also do market assessment for all the locations in order to check the market capability to satisfy people’s basic needs. Market assessment shall focus on the items and their alternative availability, and unit prices for each item. Based on the result, the distribution amount will be determined.

title.narrative: Providing quality primary education to 9,000 out-of-school children (8-11, 60% g

description.narrative: Just 37% of girls in South Sudan go to school. 6% complete primary education. Schools are far away, with few women teachers and of poor quality. Girls often end up married or pregnant very early. They live at constant risk of conflict. The project will set up 300 one-room community schools. The poorest and most at-risk children aged 8-11 (60% girls) will do three years of education and successfully move into the government system. Staff will train and support local women as teachers so they are more confident and earn their own livelihood. School Management Committees and parents’ forums will protect children better from harm.

title.narrative: Stabilization and Early Reintegration Support for Returnees in South Sudan.

description.narrative: Stabilization & Early Reintegration Support for Returnees in South Sudan The proposed projects seeks to provide community-based early reintegration support in communities that have been affected by an influx of returnees resettling back in Southern Sudan through the provision of livelihood recovery and economic reintegration. Outputs: - Livelihoods supported through provision of training in return communities, targeting a total of 1500 beneficiaries by ILO, prioritizing women/female headed households and youth. - Beneficiaries receive small grants to help them start their small business (IOM). Up to 413 recipients of ILO GYB training will receive business start up kits. Up to 300 “at risk” youth from the target area will receive vocational training courses in subject areas provide the greatest likelihood of employment following course completion. - 36 local construction company representatives from target area receive contractor training to improve competitiveness. Target: - Small-grants scheme for SMEs and vocational training opportunities established in the 3 target States. - 1500 beneficiaries receive entrepreneurship /skills training.

title.narrative: Scaling up access to quality and integrated Education and CPIE services in Pibor, Lekuangole, Verthet and Gumuruk to support vulnerable children, especially girls, adolescents and caregivers affected by violence, conflict and food insecurity (Greater Pibor Administrative Area, South Sudan).

description.narrative:
Plan will scale-up provision of quality integrated CPIE and Education services to vulnerable children, adolescents especially girls and caregivers for communities affected by conflict, violence and food insecurity in Pibor, Verteth, Gumuruk, and Lekuangole payam in Greater Pibor Administrative area for 12-months implementation period. This project will build up from the SSHF funded project in similar locations. The beneficiaries needs are based on a Plan July 2022 needs assessment, feedback from the affected population, 2022 Humanitarian Needs Overview (HNO) and 2022 Humanitarian Response Plan among others. The proposed project is in line with Child Protection and Education Area of Responsibility (CP and Education AOR) clusters priorities, Allocation Strategy and HRPs 2022 strategic priorities. The interventions will target vulnerable communities comprising of IDPs, vulnerable members of Host communities, Retunees including persons living with disability. Additionally, special attention will be given to vulnerable and excluded women, adolescent girls and vulnerable children targeting 20,220 beneficiaries (M:3207,W:4113,B:6300,G:6600), ensuring the inclusion of persons with disabilities. Highlights of the interventions per sector are provided below:-
Education: Interventions integrated with CPIE will support learners in 4 locations by providing learning/ teaching materials, rebuilding safe learning spaces, constructing gender-segregated latrines and supporting teachers, education authorities, and school management committees. Furthermore, it aims to mobilize out-of-school children to return to school through back-to-learning campaigns, awareness sessions in all 4 payam amp providing MHM to girls. The program will support 4900 school children (B:2800, G:2100) primary students. CPIE interventions will enhance protection of vulnerable children, adolescents and caregivers in Pibor, Lekuangole, Verteth and Gumuruk in Greater Pibor Administrative Area for UASC, abductees CAAFAG, Child survivors of SGBV, children with distress, out of school and in school children among others. CPIE interventions will be integrated with Education activities in schools and community Child friendly Spaces. CPIE Mainstreaming will also be done into other sectors such as GBV, Shelter, Health, Nutrition, Legal among others through provision of case management for 500 (300G, 200B) vulnerable children including adolescents, children with disability to meet their unique needs Provision of alternative family-based care and FTR for UASC/at-risk children Updating and printing of Child Protection referral pathways to ensure efficient amptimely service provision Provision of psychosocial support through structured-non structured PSS in schools, Static and mobile CFSs to support 10,000 beneficiaries (1,000M, 2,700F,3,100B,3,200G) including 200 persons with disability across all 4 locations Conducting 4 days CP and GBV capacity building to 30 CP staff, 15 caseworkers and 30 stakeholders on CPMS, safeguarding, SOPs, Information and data protocol, PFA, inclusion among others. 12 Case workers, 3 CPIE assistants and other Case management staff will be trained and coached on utilization of upgraded CPIMS+V.2 system for case management including other essential topics such as basic counselling, PSS ,Interagency and Plan International quality standardsamp guidelines 18 CFS facilitators will be trained on SBCC and community level approaches. Structured and joint awareness with Education, CPWG and other sectors will benefit 15,000 beneficiaries (M:3,000, W:4000, B:3500boys, G:4500). Protection monitoring on protection will be done by all trained community structures for CPIE

description.narrative: Verbesserung der Gesundheitsversorgung für die Bevölkerung im Südsudan

Menschen in schwierigen Lebensbedingungen und Armutslagen sterben überdurchschnittlich viele Menschen an vermeidbaren Todesursachen auf Grund von mangelhafter Gesundheitsversorgung. Das Projekt möchte daher einen Beitrag zu einer qualitativ guten, präventiven und kurativen Gesundheitsversorgung der Bevölkerung leisten. Zielgruppe sind Betreibende kleinständiger landwirtschaftlicher Unternehmen. Mit Hilfe der Fördermittel können sie mit notwenidigen Behandlungen in verschiedenen medizinischen Fachbereichen versorgt werden.

People in difficult living conditions and poverty situations die in above-average numbers from preventable causes of death due to inadequate health care. The project therefore aims to contribute to good quality, preventive and curative health care for the population. The target group is operators of small agricultural enterprises. With the help of the subsidies, they can be provided with necessary treatments in various medical fields.

title.narrative: Envelope 1: Support for people affected by food insecurity in IPC 4 and 5 areas - Duk, Twic East, Bor South, Jonglei State and Rumbek North, Lakes State, South Sudan.

description.narrative: The Republic of South Sudan – the world’s youngest nation – has been plagued by multiple hazards including conflict, catastrophic flooding for the second year in the row, inter-communal violence, displacement, economic crisis, pest and diseases, invasion of desert locust, and the COVID-19 pandemic. In response to last Integrated Phase Classification (IPC) release, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the UN (FAO) has launched its 2021 Emergency Livelihood Response Programme (ELRP) Scale up Plan to save lives, enhance household livelihood, own food production and reduce their annual food gap, decrease the degree and frequency with which households depend on external food assistance, and strengthen their capacity to absorb shocks. Given the gravity of the food security situation in the months to come and recent needs assessments, FAO and implementing partners, namely AVSI Foundation, the Lutheran World Federation (LWF), and Green Belt Initiative (BGI) will provide livelihood response during dry season targeting people affected by food insecurity in IPC 4 locations. The project will be implemented by LWF in Twic East (Kongor, Lith, Pakeer, Nyuak, Ajoung payams and river islands), GBI in Duk (payams:Ageer, Dongchak,Padiet, Pagak, Panyang and Payue), FAO field office in Bor South (payams: Bor, Kolyang, Makuach, Anyidi, Baidit and Jalle) in Jonglei State, and AVSI in Rumbek North (payams Maper, Madol, Malueeth, Aloor, Wunrieng and Meen), Lakes State. A total of 204 192 people will be supported with combination of vegetable and fishing kits, agriculture hand tools and trainings. The response will address the needs of food insecure population from the targeted locations, specifically focusing on providing assorted fast-maturing vegetable kits (5-7 types of vegetable seeds), fishing kit (hooks, monofilament, twines), agriculture hand tools (maloda, rake or hoe), and additional watering cans and water pumps. This intervention will allow affected population access the food immediately through fishing activities and within short period of 7 weeks for vegetable production. To complement livelihood kits distributions, the project will train beneficiaries in improved agronomic and fishing practices, including reducing postharvest losses, and cross cutting themes such as nutrition. The establishment of the vegetable gardens will help to promote best agriculture practices. The project will also establish vegetable gardens next to 1 nutrition centers and 1 school in Twic East. The trainings in best agronomic practices will be further supported by dissemination of information through the Public Service Announcements (PSA) in local language in the local radio station funded by complementary FAO's ELRP projects. The intervention will address gender equalities with regards to women’s access to productive assets by providing them with tailored portable livelihood packages of vegetables increasing their knowledge on agriculture production and finally addressing women’s work burden in agriculture by providing time-saving equipment’s such to reduce the drudgery of water collection and providing irrigation for household vegetable gardens, and enable women to use their time more productively. Beneficiaries will include Internally Displaced Persons (IDP), host communities, returnees, and community vulnerable groups’ representatives (female headed household, households with malnourished children, single mothers widows, elders, handicapped or chronically ill, refugee, youth at risk, survivors of GBV). Overall, the project will target a total of 204 192 people, of which 181 392 people will receive vegetable kits packages (seeds and tool), 183 405 people will receive fishing kits, 3 764 people (including 400 children) will be trained in best agronomic practices, and 1 488 will receive training in fisheries.

title.narrative: Increasing access and strengthening capacities of PHC to provide emergency lifesaving health care services in Fangak, Panyijiar, Duk, and Magwi counties, Bentiu PoC and Juba PoC through the provision of two mobile units.

description.narrative: WHO leads integrated disease surveillance, risk assessment investigation, confirmation and initial response to outbreaks with support from other partners. Given that the emergency response partners only deploy teams after an outbreak has been confirmed, there is need to ensure that initial response alongside investigations and assessments during the pre-confirmation period is strengthened to provide immediate integrated health, WaSH and nutrition services as a means of mitigating the impact of health events, outbreaks and ultimately reducing preventable deaths. WHO will respond in Fangak, Panyijiar, Duk, and Magwi counties, Bentiu PoC and Juba PoC, through the provision of two mobile units, and also cover all the other Health Cluster priority locations on need basis with emphasis on the 8 earmarked for integrated approach with three other Clusters. At a cost of $500 000, WHO will target to reach 221 056 beneficiaries. The money will be allocated proportionately as follows: Fangak county $51629, Panyijiar county $9796, Magwi county $36412, Duk county $55800, Bentiu PoC $259398, and Juba PoC $86964. It is expected that these interventions will complement already ongoing activities by MoH and bilateral funding to partners.

title.narrative: Addressing acute Water, Sanitation and Hygiene needs of vulnerable and disaster affected population of Leer county and Rubkway payam of Mayendit county, Southern Unity State

description.narrative: Addressing acute Water, Hygiene and Sanitation needs of vulnerable and disaster affected population of Leer and Rubkuay payam in Mayendit North Count in Unity State is paramount due to the fact that the population using water points are more than the standard required because the water points are few. The overuse contributes to breakdown of the pumps and reduction in water availability. Due to the fact that the current water supply situation is below standards in quality and quantity of 500 people (women, men, boys and girls) per borehole approximately 1,000 people (women, men, boys and girls) served by one hand pump, resulting in a limited amount of boreholes and water supply schemes which also results in overuse, which contributes to breakdown of the pumps and reduction in water availability. This leads not only to low water consumption (under 10 L/person/day) but also increases the burden of women and girls caretakers who solely walk for more than five(5)km fetching water exposing them to some forms of GBV namely abduction of young girls and boys, forceful marriages, killing and rape of young girls. Due to the fact that houses and sketchy sanitation structures were destroyed within the communities by the recent conflict. The current hygiene and sanitation structures merely exist exposing the residents to open defecation posing an extreme public health problem especially water borne diseases e.g. diarrhea and cholera. The project aims to rehabilitate 15 non-functioning boreholes in Mayendit North county(Rupkuay,Kuok,Thaker payams and Tunyang boma) so that the population can access water at an average of 1,000 people (women, men, boys and girls) per borehole which is above the standard quality requirement but is far better than the current average usage of 1,984 per borehole as reported in OCHA led IRNA report for June 2014 before even the recent conflict of May 2015 to December 2015. A total 16,000 people (women, men, boys and girls) will benefit through provision of access to water by rehabilitation and repair of 15 boreholes and improve sanitation through hygiene promotion.There is a need for maintenance of hygienic conditions and hygiene promotion in both Lerr and Mayendit north(Rupkway through services of human waste management, improved toilets, water facilities, and waste disposal, hygiene promotion campaigns to raise awareness on water-related health/hygiene issues, especially to raise awareness on safe water and cholera prevention.

description.narrative: the proposed intervention aims at: i) providing food security and livelihood support, to the vulnerable urban populations affected by market shocks, through access to some space for home gardening or vertical gardening with vegetable production inputs to produce nutritious vegetables; ii) reducing the health risks of COVID-19 transmission in the markets by promoting adequate measures on sanitation and hygiene through the provision of PPE to market vendors and mobile washing hands facilities; spraying of markets and provision of protective gear; as well as fast tracking of the construction of water infrastructures in the market areas; iii) supporting the food value chain and income generation for vulnerable women traders through cash for restocking their capacities. In addition to these priority areas, other activities will be integrated to address gender inequalities and the vulnerability of Gender Based Violence (GBV), especially domestic violence that the COVID-19 has deepen.

title.narrative: Provision of Multipurpose Cash (MPC) to Communities Affected by the Food Insecurity in South Sudan

description.narrative: According to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), more than 230,000 individuals in Fangak and Pibor Counties in South Sudan are currently facing food insecurity due to climatic shocks (floods and droughts), conflict, economic downturn, displacement, and disrupted livelihoods. In this project, IOM is providing multi-purpose cash assistance to the most vulnerable populations classified as catastrophic/level 5 of the IPC. The multipurpose cash assistance enables and provides flexibility to the most vulnerable populations to address their food insecurity needs and compliments the wider humanitarian response beyond food distribution and other non-food-items and water, sanitation and hygiene needs which arise due to food insecurity.

description.narrative:
Omprogrammerade medel för att lindra konsekvenserna av covid-19 Detta beslut avser stöd till Oxfam GB för humanitära projekt genom ett nytt avtal mellan Sida och Oxfam GB för perioden april 2018 – juni 2021.
Under 2018 kommer fler än 135 miljoner människor vara i behov av humanitärt bistånd världen över till en kostnad av 22,5 miljarder dollar enligt United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA). Sveriges humanitära bistånd är behovsbaserat och Sida genomför i enlighet med detta årligen en humanitär allokeringsprocess, vari samtliga humanitära kriser analyseras utifrån de humanitära behoven och där de mest relevanta av strategiska partnerorganisationer att svara upp mot identifierade behov utväljs.
Ett flertal av de identifierade globala behoven för 2018 återfinns i utdragna och bortglömda kriser och Sida bedömer att Oxfam GB är väl positionerad att svara upp mot dessa behov i kraft av att organisationen även arbetar med långsiktigt utvecklingssamarbete, har god kännedom om den lokala kontexten i samtliga föreslagna projekt samt genom att kapacitetsstärkande av lokala aktörer är centralt i Oxfam GB’s humanitära arbete. År 2018–2021 föreslås därför att Oxfam GB, utöver stöd för akut livräddande aktiviteter, även erhåller finansiering för mer långsiktiga aktiviteter i syfte att stärka samhällens motståndskraft mot kriser och katastrofer.
Oxfam GB har under tidigare samarbeten med Sida, senast genom stöd under avtalsperioden 2011–2013 samt 2014–2017, påvisat att organisationen är en effektiv humanitär aktör. Enbart under 2016 lyckades Oxfam GB nå 1,2 miljoner människor med stöd inom vatten, sanitet och hygien, 94 000 människor med tryggad livsmedelsförsörjning och förbättrade försörjningsmöjligheter samt bidra med stärkt skydd för 106 000 människor i konfliktdrabbade miljöer. Sida bedömer i linje med detta att Oxfam GB framförallt har ett mervärde vad gäller aktiviteter inom tryggad livsmedelsförsörjning, genom matdistribution och kontantbaserat stöd; försörjningsmöjligheter, bland annat genom stöd till återhämtning inom boskapsskötsel och jordbruk; vatten, sanitet och hygien, både genom akut livräddande aktiviteter och långsiktiga aktiviteter i syfte att stärka vattensystem; samt skydd, såväl genom integrering av skydd i exempelvis matdistribution som specifika skyddsaktiviteter i syfte att exempelvis öka medvetenheten om könsbaserat våld. Oxfam arbetar även aktivt med påverkansarbete kring internationell humanitär rätt och de humanitära principerna.
År 2018-2021 planerar Oxfam GB att nå över 280 000 personer i Algeriet, Centralafrikanska republiken, Demokratiska republiken Kongo, Irak och Tchad. Insatsen kommer bestå av fyra komponenter med fokus på akut livräddande aktiviteter; projekt i syfte att stärka samhällens motståndskraft mot kriser och katastrofer; möjlighet att snabbt svara upp mot hastigt uppkomna behov i nya kriser eller akuta försämringar av pågående kriser inom ramen för snabbinsatsmekanismen RRM; samt stärkt effektivitet i det humanitära systemet genom metodstöd som syftar till att öka kunskapen om kontantbaserat stöd.
Sida bedömer att Oxfam GB’s planerade projekt svarar mot aktuella humanitära behov i enlighet med Sidas geografiska analys och stöd till den föreslagna insatsen bedöms som relevant för att uppnå målen i Strategi för Sveriges humanitära bistånd genom Styrelsen för internationellt utvecklingssamarbete (Sida) 2017–2020. Sida föreslår därför att stödja Oxfam GB’s humanitära projekt till en kostnad av 104 MSEK i enlighet med följande:
Landprojekt
Två 1-åriga projekt föreslås finansieras med totalt 5 MSEK med följande fördelning:
Demokratiska republiken Kongo: 1 MSEK I Demokratiska republiken Kongo planerar Oxfam GB att stödja ett INGO-forum med 100 icke-statliga medlemsorganisationer i syfte att öka effektiviteten av humanitärt bistånd genom stärkt samordning.
Irak: 4 MSEK I Irak föreslås att Sida stödjer ett projekt som riktar sig till 9 600 personer med livräddande aktiviteter inom bland annat vatten, sanitet och hygien samt tryggad livsmedelsförsörjning genom exempelvis distribution av hygienartiklar, mat och andra basala förnödenheter.
Fem 3-åriga projekt föreslås finansieras med totalt 28 MSEK för 2018, 19 MSEK för 2019 samt 16 MSEK för 2020 med följande fördelning:
Algeriet: 15 MSEK (5+5+5 MSEK) I Algeriet planerar Oxfam GB att stödja 126 600 västsahariska flyktingar i ett projekt som fokuserar på tryggad livsmedelsförsörjning och stärkt motståndskraft mot framtida kriser och katastrofer, genom bland annat distribution av färska grönsaker och introduktion av klimatanpassade grödor.
Centralafrikanska republiken: 18 MSEK (10+5+3 MSEK) I Centralafrikanska republiken planerar Oxfam GB att nå 17 500 personer från de mest utsatta konfliktdrabbade grupperna i två projekt med aktiviteter inom tryggad livsmedelsförsörjning, skydd samt vatten, sanitet och hygien, genom exempelvis distribution av jordbruksredskap, utbildning i syfte att stärka kunskapen om diversifierad kosthållning samt skyddsaktiviteter, bland annat bestående av kapacitetsstärkning av skyddskommittéer.
Tchad: 18 MSEK (10+5+3 MSEK) I Tchad planerar Oxfam GB att stödja 49 087 människor, inklusive internflyktingar och personer från värdsamhällen, med aktiviteter inom skydd samt vatten, sanitet och hygien. Projektverksamheten innefattar bland annat brunnsborrning, utbildning inom vatten, sanitet och hygien samt konstruktion av latriner. Projektet kommer även inkludera inrättande av skyddskommittéer samt aktiviteter som syftar till att öka medvetenheten om könsbaserat våld.
Irak: 12 MSEK (3+4+5 MSEK) I Irak förslås stöd till ett kapacitetsstärkande projekt av lokala humanitära organisationer samt ett antal lokala civilsamhällsorganisationer i syfte att förbättra den lokala responskapaciteten och därmed stärka lokalsamhällets motståndskraft mot framtida kriser och katastrofer.
Rapid Response Mechanism
Vidare föreslås att Sida bidrar med 25 MSEK inom ramen för snabbinsatsmekanismen RRM för att möjliggöra för Oxfam GB att snabbt svara upp mot hastigt uppkomna behov i nya kriser eller akuta försämringar av pågående kriser.
Metodstöd
Ett metodprojekt till Cash Learning Partnership (CaLP) föreslås finansieras med totalt 4 MSEK för 2018, 3 MSEK för 2019 samt 2 MSEK för 2019:
CaLP är ett nätverk som arbetar med lärande, kunskapsdelning, nätverkande och koordination gällande kontantbaserat stöd. Mot bakgrund av att Sida i samband med World Humanitarian Summit och Grand Bargain åtagit sig att stärka arbetet med kontantbaserat stöd, rekommenderas i denna beredning att inkludera stöd till CaLP. Detta stöd ingår i beredningen av Oxfam GB eftersom CaLP inte är en egen juridisk person utan återfinns inom Humanitarian Department of Oxfam House.
Sida föreslår även att finansiera Oxfam GB’s programhanteringskostnader till en total kostnad av 2 MSEK för 2018. Programhanteringskostnaderna täcker en programkoordinator (100%), en finansiell funktion (75%), en programansvarig (100%), tekniskt rådgivande stöd (inom exempelvis tryggad livsmedelsförsörjning och skydd) samt fältuppföljning och externa revisionskostnader. Sida bedömer att programhanteringskostnaderna är nödvändiga för att säkra kvaliteten på hanteringen av Sida-medlen eftersom delar av de administrativa kostnaderna på 7% vidarebefordras till andra delar av Oxfams federation och därmed inte kommer Oxfam GB till del.
För detaljerad överblick och fördelning av Sidas stöd hänvisas till avtalets bilaga VII (Budget summary).
Även om Sida bedömer att Oxfam GB har god kapacitet att implementera humanitära projekt har Sida under tidigare samarbeten noterat vissa svagheter vad gäller intern styrning och kontroll, framförallt vad gäller revision, vidareförmedling samt finansiell rapportering. Sida kommer därför under 2018 att följa hur väl Oxfam GB åtgärdar brister inom dessa områden.
Med anledning av de uppmärksammade fallen där Oxfam GB’s personal varit inblandade i sexuellt utnyttjande och andra brott mot organisationens etiska principer, har Sida efterfrågat detaljerad information om de åtgärder Oxfam GB vidtagit sedan dessa händelser ägde rum år 2010, inklusive en detaljerad redogörelse för hur de vidtagna åtgärderna fungerat i praktiken. De erhållna svaren visar att Oxfam GB tagit frågan på stort allvar och att man sedan år 2010 har etablerat verkningsfulla regler och rutiner, som man under år 2018 dessutom planerar att skärpa ytterligare. Sida bedömer att de svar som erhållits är tillräckliga för att Sida ska kunna ingå ett nytt treårsavtal med Oxfam GB.
Vidare bedömer Sida att samtliga medel för projekten ska utbetalas omgående för att möjliggöra planering och uppstart av projekten till 1 april 2018. Detta för att på bästa sätt möjliggöra omedelbar uppstart av de humanitära aktiviteterna. Ett avsteg från Sidas vanliga rutiner om uppdelade betalningar bedöms motiverat.
Bedömningspromemorian har skrivits på engelska med anledning av att engelskspråkig personal i fält är delaktig i beredning och uppföljning av insatsen, i enlighet med Generaldirektörens beslut om Sidas språkvalsmatris med tillämpningsanvisningar från den 1 mars 2013.

Reprogrammed funds to mitigate the impact of COVID-19 In 2018-2021, Oxfam GB plans to reach over 280,000 people in Algeria, the Central African Republic, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Iraq and Chad. The contribution will consist of four components focusing on emergency life-saving activities; multi-year resilience building projects; the possibility to respond to sudden onset or deteriorating humanitarian emergencies during the year through the Rapid Response Mechanism; as well as support to method development of cash-based programming.In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Oxfam will provide support to an INGO forum with 100 NGO members with the aim of increasing the effectiveness of humanitarian interventions through improved coordination. In Iraq, Sida will support a project focusing on first line emergency response. The projects will target 9,600 people and include activities of food distribution as well as distribution of non-food items and hygiene materials.Five 3-year projects are proposed to be funded with a total of 28 MSEK for 2018, 19 MSEK for 2019 and 16 MSEK for 2019 with the following breakdown:In Algeria, 126 600 Sahrawi refugees will be supported in a project focusing on improving dietary diversity and strengthening of small-scale agriculture with the aim of increasing food security in the refugee camps. To reach the planned goals of the project, Oxfam will distribute fresh vegetables and flour, conduct trainings and awareness sessions on agricultural production and introduce drought-resistant crops.In the Central African Republic, Oxfam will target 17,500 people with food, protection and WASH activities, together with resilience building through recovery of productive assets and strengthening of communities’ conflict management capabilities. The proposed activities include distribution of agricultural kits, awareness-raising on food diversification, protection and gender themes as well as strengthening of community protection committees.The project in Chad will target 49,087 people in a project aiming to improve access to basic social services, protection, and the restoration of livelihoods. The project activities include borehole drilling, trainings of water management committees, latrine construction and hygiene promotion. The project will also highlight issues of protection and gender-based violence through awareness raising, establishment of protection committees, mapping of care services for victims of abuses and violations and awareness raising sessions on protection issues.In Iraq, Sida will support a project focusing on capacity building of local humanitarian leadership with the aim of strengthening the local humanitarian response capacity. The projects will target local humanitarian actors as well as a number of local NGOs. Moreover, it is further proposed that Sida contributes with 25 million within the Rapid Response Mechanism, RRM, to enable Oxfam GB to respond to sudden onset or deteriorating humanitarian emergencies throughout the year.Moreover, in addition to funding provided directly to Oxfam GB, Sida will also support the Cash Learning Partnership (CaLP) in a 3-year intervention with a total funding of 9 MSEK (4+3+2 MSEK). CaLP is a network based on learning, knowledge sharing, networking and coordination around the appropriate and timely use of cash transfer programming (CTP) in humanitarian response. CaLP does not deliver cash transfer programmes directly. The vision of CaLP is that humanitarian assistance creates the greatest value, choice and dignity for people in crisis.

Fewer women, men and children will die or suffer from a loss of dignity through insecurity and deprivation by reducing the impact of natural disasters and conflict and strengthening the resilience of communities and local partners.

description.narrative:
Over 1,393,031 affected women, men, girls and boys have been reached through 38 projects in 20 countries under the 2018-2021 HPA with activities in Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH), Emergency Food Security and Vulnerable Livelihoods (EFSVL), Gender and Protection. Women and girls represented more than 50% of the beneficiaries.
As mentioned in the previous section, during the HPA II, Oxfam implemented five multiyear projects; six annual planned projects and method and capacity development projects in CAR and the global Cash Learning project named CaLP. Oxfam also implemented 27 RRM responses.
Through RRM responses, Oxfam reached more than 724,000 people with a total of 97,600,062 SEK. Sida funded Oxfam Rapid Emergency Responses in Bangladesh, Syria, Senegal, Mauritania, Somaliland (x2), CAR (x2), Afghanistan (x2), Niger, Burkina, Malawi, Mozambique, Sudan Sudan (x2), Kenya (x3), Chad (x3), Western Sahara, Iraq, Colombia, Honduras, Guatemala.
Oxfam used nearly 80% of the RRM projects to respond to natural disasters such as: floods, cyclones, locust infestations, droughts and the COVID-19 pandemic. Two RRM projects responded to political crises: the Venezuela migrant crisis in Colombia and the closure of refugee camps in Iraq. Five RRM responses were conflict related (Syria, CAR (x2), Niger and Burkina Faso). More than half of the RRM projects (16), Oxfam implemented together with local humanitarian partners in alignment with the Grand Bargain and Charter for Change Commitments to localisation.
Examples of some of the concrete results achieved in the past agreement period include: - In CAR 12 water points were rehabilitated providing access to water for 7,000 people and also preventing spread of waterborne diseases. - In the first year of the HPA agreement in Syria, through the supply of water pumps and rehabilitation of wells and water points, 129,789 people displaced by conflict in Dar'a, Syria, have got access to adequate and safe water. - In Somaliland, 12,000 vulnerable drought affected persons received two rounds of unconditional cash transfers providing them access to basic requirements such as food, clothing and medication, as part of re-establishing their livelihoods base. - In Niger, following attacks on several villages causing widespread displacement, Oxfam revitalized community protection mechanisms in 12 IDP sites and improved the protection of particularly women and children. - In Algeria in 2020, 133,672 vulnerable Sahrawi refugees were supported with improved food security during COVID-19-related restrictions on movement and impacts on markets through the distribution of 2.5 kg of fresh produce over 3 months. A final year evaluation of the project in Algeria showed that approximately 81% of the agricultural production realised through the establishment of communal gardens was used for commercial purposes and 19% for household consumption. The proceeds from resale went towards buying other types of food, buying seeds and agricultural inputs or improvements of overall living conditions of the household. - In CAR Paoua, the multiyear project showed a significant reduction in the number of recorded protection cases, including 73% of rapes were recorded before and 63% at the end; 72% of physical violence before and 40.80% at the end, 36% of abductions before and 10.20% at the end. - For the project in Chad in 2020, 44,593 people were reached through information on protection, the construction of 12 community protection spaces, distribution of 100 solar lamps to women and girls and other protection services. Community structures and committees and the creation of dialogue between them and the local authorities and training sessions have contributed considerably to reducing protection risks, and improving knowledge and the actions taken in this respect: 98.33% of male and female protection committee members took positive actions against protection threats and risks during the project. There was also a 23.69% reduction in protection cases and threats compared with last year and 93.22% of protection incidents referred to the authorities were resolved. - In both the multi-year projects in Chad and CAR, capacity building and advocacy around protection made noticeable progress because of the extended duration of the projects. Protection Committees are playing a more active role in victims referrals and coordination with other protection actors is stronger. - With regards to the CaLP project, 98% of respondents felt that CaLPs work has improved CVA coordination a great deal, a lot or a moderate amount and 88% of respondents reported that CaLP research, tools or guidance increased the quality of their organizations programming.
