description.narrative:
Detta beslut och tillhörande beredning avser en ny insats (Beslut om insats, Insatshanteringsregeln 2.9 §) mellan Sida och Rädda Barnens Riksförbund (Rädda Barnen) för avtalsperioden 2021-2025. Beslutet och tillhörande beredning avser dessutom stöd till Rädda Barnens humanitära verksamhet under 2021 (stöd för avtalsåren 2022-2025 är avhängligt Sidas godkännande av Rädda Barnens fullständiga ansökan för respektive år enligt att-satserna ovan). Stödet för 2021 avser sex kriser (Irak, Mali, Mocambique, Sydsudan, Syrien och Jemen). Det syftar dessutom till att möjliggöra för Rädda Barnen att genom Sida's snabbinsatsmekanism (Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM)) svara upp mot plötsligt uppkomna eller kraftigt förvärrade humanitära kriser under 2021. Därutöver syftar det till att stärka Rädda Barnens kapacitet; möjliggöra för Rädda Barnen att stärka det humanitära systemet; samt bidra till Rädda Barnens operationella och tekniska kapacitet på huvudkontoret i Stockholm.
Aktuellt beslut omfattar finansiellt stöd till Rädda Barnen om 99 393 000 SEK under 2021.
Målet med insatsen (2021-2025) är att bidra till tre "Förändringar" (Breakthroughs) som identifierats inom Save the Children-rörelsen som del av dess vision för 2030. Dessa är att barn ska:
1. Överleva - inga barn dör av orsaker som kan förebyggas innan de fyllt fem år. 2. Lära - alla barn får del av kvalitativ grundläggande utbildning. 3. Vara skyddade - våld mot barn tolereras inte längre.
I ljuset av Sveriges "Strategi för Sveriges humanitära bistånd genom Styrelsen för internationellt utvecklingssamarbete (Sida) 2021-2025" kommer särskilt den tredje Förändringen - vara skyddade - att vara central, eftersom ett av strategins huvudmål är "Förbättrad förmåga att tillgodose skydd och assistans för krisdrabbade människor". Rädda Barnen kommer dessutom i hög utsträckning att integrera skyddskomponenter i sin multisektoriella assistans inom ramen för insatsens tema "Centrality of Protection". Detta tema syftar till att på ett holistiskt sätt minska skyddsrelaterade risker och svara upp mot skyddsrelaterade behov hos barn i kombination med andra projektkomponenter, snarare än att betrakta skydd som isolerat från andra delmål.

During 2020, Sida's Unit for Humanitarian Assistance conducted an overview of ongoing strategic partnerships in order to ensure that partnerships were established with the most relevant and effective humanitarian actors to carry out Sida's Humanitarian Strategy. As a result of the overview, Sida has decided to appraise a new contribution and enter into a new strategic partnership agreement with Save the Children Sweden (SCS) for the period 2021-2025 (see archive number 2021-000057).
In 2021, the following is proposed in support to SCS: Annual Projects in line with Humanitarian Response Plans (12 months) - SEK 63 million; Rapid Response Mechanism support - SEK 25 million; Capacity Building and Method Development support - SEK 5.593 million; Surge Support - SEK 800,000; and Operational and Technical Support to SCS's HQ - SEK 5 million.
This means that the total initial contribution to SCS in 2021 would amount to SEK 99,393,000.
The overall objective of the intervention is to contribute to the promotion of three Breakthroughs in the way children are treated in the world: Survive, Learn and Be Protected. These are part of the Save the Children movement's Vision for 2030 and are defined as remarkable and sustainable shifts from current trends that Save the Children aspires to work to achieve for children. Their respective objective is the following:
1. Survive: No child dies of preventable causes before their fifth birthday. 2. Learn: All children learn from quality basic education. 3. Be Protected: Violence against children is no longer tolerated.
One of the main comparative advantages of Save the Children is its competence in addressing protection-related concerns. For this reason, Centrality of Protection has been proposed as the thematic frame, making the Be Protected Breakthrough particularly central for its interventions during the agreement period.
Finally, in addition to these three Breakthroughs, the proposed contribution also aligns with Sweden's newly adopted "Strategy for Sweden’s humanitarian assistance provided through the Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency (Sida) 2021–2025".

Vision, Humanitarian Policy and Humanitarian Plan The overall objective of the intervention is to contribute to the promotion of three Breakthroughs in the way children are treated in the world: Survive, Learn and Be Protected. These are part of the Save the Children movement's Vision for 2030 and are defined as remarkable and sustainable shifts from current trends that Save the Children aspires to work to achieve for children. Their respective objective is the following: Survive: No child dies of preventable causes before their fifth birthday. Learn: All children learn from quality basic education. Be Protected: Violence against children is no longer tolerated. For the upcoming agreement period 2021-2025, SCS has identified several aims under each breakthrough that it seeks to promote with Sida's humanitarian funding. All Country Offices within Save the Children are to be held accountable for their contribution to the Breakthroughs through a combination of programming, promotion, advocacy, funding and public mobilization. This is assessed to require integrated expertise in health, nutrition, education, child protection, child poverty and child rights governance. The work will be undertaken by SCS as part of both its development and humanitarian programming. The humanitarian sphere of work related to the Breakthroughs is anchored in the Save the Children movement's Humanitarian Policy - Our Approach to Humanitarian Action, adopted in 2019. It stipulates that Save the Children aims to deliver humanitarian assistance that is timely, appropriate, effective and accountable to the most vulnerable children, their families and communities. Furthermore, during 2021, the work is guided in particular by its Humanitarian Plan 2021 - Children Cannot Wait. The plan is structured around four pillars, of which the first three align with the three strategic Breakthroughs: Child Survival, Access to Education, and Child Protection. The fourth pillar is Avoid Negative Coping Mechanisms, which sets out the aim for Save the Children to promote increased income opportunities, CVA for basic needs, in-kind food when CVA is not appropriate, as well as government social protection schemes. The overarching ambition of the Plan is for Save the Children to respond to the humanitarian needs of 15.7 million people, including 9.4 million children, in 2021. Finally, to achieve the Breakthroughs, Save the Children emphasizes the importance of standards in its programming. For this reason, its Humanitarian Policy commits the organization to ensure that its programming consistently aligns with and integrates the Core Humanitarian Standards (CHS), the Sphere standards, the Inter- Agency Network for Education In Emergencies (INEE) minimum standards, and the Child Protection Minimum Standards (CPMS). Centrality of Protection In 2019, a Centrality of Protection policy and strategy was endorsed in line with the Interagency Standing Committee (IASC) Principles Statement on the Centrality of Protection in Humanitarian Action (2013). Through the statement, protection became recognized as the purpose and intended outcome of humanitarian action. For Save the Children, the commitment to Centrality of Protection is built around six policy statements: 1. Ensure capacity of humanitarian staff to understand, recognise and respond to violations of International Humanitarian Law/International Human Rights Law/International Refugee Law/International Criminal Law and uphold humanitarian principles in humanitarian crises. 2. Adopt a conflict-sensitive approach to the centrality of protection. 3. Systematize the approach to child protection analysis and integration in humanitarian crises. 4. Commit to the identification, response, monitoring and reporting of grave and other serious child rights violations. 5. Define the organizational position and develop an appropriate response when identifying the erosion of the international legal framework for upholding child rights in humanitarian contexts. 6. Strengthen interagency collaboration, including as a Cluster Lead agency, and use that to promote child rights within the humanitarian protection architecture. For SCS's Sida-funded Humanitarian Program 2021-2025, Centrality of Protection has been proposed as the thematic frame, making the Be Protected breakthrough particularly central for its interventions. It would entail a broader conceptualization of protection than during the agreement period 2017-2020, which had the thematic frame Children and Armed Conflict, with a specific focus on Protecting Children in Conflict. The key difference would be moving beyond preventing protection risks faced by children through child protection-focused interventions, towards integrating the mitigation of protection risks into all SCS's sectors of work whenever relevant. The ambition is to promote a more comprehensive and holistic approach to addressing child protection concerns in contrast to doing so in isolation. Initial Allocation 2021 In alignment with Save the Children's ambitions related to its Vision for 2030 and the three strategic Breakthroughs, its Humanitarian Policy, its Humanitarian Plan, as well as Sida's Humanitarian Strategy, SCS has submitted a Full Project Proposal to Sida for 2021. Sida has reviewed these proposals and drawn the conclusion that they align well with the abovementioned priorities as well as the proposed Centrality of Protection thematic frame. Below, a short description is provided for the proposed projects to be supported by Sida as part of the initial allocation 2021. The activity period for each project is 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2022, which corresponds to the 2021 work year. I. Annual Projects (in line with the most recent Humanitarian Response Plans) Iraq - SEK 15,000,000 Three years after the end of Iraq’s conflict against ISIS, the impacts of fighting remain high. In 2020, more than 4.1 million people were in need of some form of humanitarian assistance, and it is estimated that over 2.3. million individuals will be in need of protection services in 2021. Moreover, 1.3 million people are estimated to be internally displaced, many of whom facing additional vulnerabilities as a result of the Government of Iraq's announcement in October 2020 that all camps and informal locations for Internally Displaced People (IDP) are to be closed. Save the Children has significant experience of addressing humanitarian needs in Iraq. In their activities, they include capacity strengthening for the Department of Labour and Social Affairs and other local actors working with child protection-related issues. Furthermore, Save the Children has a strong localization focus, with 40 % of the funds designated for the proposed intervention planned for to be forwarded to the three local implementing partners: Harikar; Al Sorouh for Sustainable Development Foundation; and Sahara Economic Development Organization. Save the Children has previously reported good results from their interventions in Iraq and has contributed to the reduction of protection risks that vulnerable girls and boys and their caregivers face. Moreover, Save the Children is co-lead in the Child Protection sub-cluster and has a role to play in the future transition to development interventions in this area of work. The project would be implemented in Ninewa (Mosul), Diyala (Mugidadia) and Dohuk (Sakho) with IDPs, recent returnees and vulnerable host communities as the targeted groups. The overall objective is to support the most vulnerable conflict-affected and displaced to survive and be protected through integrated protection, mental health and psychosocial support services, livelihoods and health actions. In alignment with the three Strategic Objectives of the draft HRP for 2021, this would be done by, inter alia, providing case management and positive parenting support services (benefitting 3,420 children and youth), multipurpose cash grants (1,320 children and 660 adults), life skills trainings (300 youth), promoting health awareness (3,000 children and 10,000 community members) and capacitating local actors to lead protection-oriented responses (520 persons). Mali - SEK 7,000,000 Of the estimated 13.5 million crisis-affected Malians, around 7.1 million are projected to be in need of humanitarian assistance in 2021 - an increase of 39 percent compared to 2020. Of these people, 3.5 million are estimated to be children. The worst affected region is Mopti, where approximately 42 % of the country's 311,193 IDPs reside (55 % of whom are women), food insecurity is pervasive and severe protection risks exist. The dire situation is mainly a result of different types of ongoing armed violence, but is compounded by poverty, weak state presence and climate change. In alignment with the first three Strategic Objectives of the 2020 HRP, the proposed intervention targets 8,940 people living in Koro and Bankass circles in Mopti region (4,700 children and 3,790 adults). It is an integrated protection intervention with a strong focus on promoting sustained outcomes. The objective is to restore the psychosocial well-being and addressing the basic needs of populations affected by the armed violence as well as to strengthen the protective environment in the region. This would be done through the provision of protection and education services, cash assistance during the lean season, and the implementation of the protection cluster's Centrality of Protection action plan. Of the budget, 60 % is designated for direct implementation by Save the Children, and the remainder for a planned partnership with a local organization. The partner organization is yet to be identified, and Sida is currently in dialogue with SCS related to this risk and potential contingency planning. Capacity building and material support is also planned for to local state actors and community groups for them to sustain the protection support structure in Mopti following the finalization of the project. This includes developing an exit plan to be implemented during the last three months of the project (January to March 2022). Mozambique - SEK 6,000,000 Ever since cyclone Kenneth struck the Cabo Delgado province in northern Mozambique in April 2019 causing widespread destruction, humanitarian needs have continued to increase. The main reason for this has been the parallel escalation of an armed conflict in the province that dawned in 2017. Between March and November 2020 alone, the number of IDPs quadrupled from around 110,400 to nearly 530,000. In total, over 1.3 million people are projected to be in need of humanitarian support in the province during 2021. Sida has provided support to Save the Children for responding to humanitarian needs in Cabo Delgado since cyclone Kenneth in 2019 and is diversifying its partner portfolio from 2021. The proposed support for Save the Children aligns specifically with the third strategic objective of the 2021 HRP - addressing protection risks and needs of crisis-affected people. As such, it is foremostly a focused rather than an integrated intervention, and targets 33,346 people (13,338 children) in the districts of Chuire, Metuge, Montepuez and Pemba. The intervention is planned for to be implemented in partnership with CARE International throught he COSACA consortium, which has been operating in Mozambique since 2007. It is focused around two Outcomes: child protection (led by Save the Children) and gender-based violence (led by CARE International. The overarching aim is to ensure crisis-affected people are protected and better able to withstand protection risks of current and future crises. Activities include case management support for unaccompanied and separated children as well as children exposed to Gender-Based Violence (GBV), and the provision of Psychosocial Support Services at Child Friendly Spaces. South Sudan - SEK 10,000,000 In South Sudan, approximately 80 % of the population of 11.8 million live on less than USD 1 per day, with an estimated 8.3 million to be in need of humanitarian assistance and 7.7 million to experience food insecurity (IPC 3 or worse). One of the worst affected states is Jonglei where the armed conflict intensified in 2020, and where needs were compounded by the Covid-19 pandemic as well as floods. The latter in particular, and volatile weather and climate change in general, pose significant threats to many South Sudanese as the majority of the population rely on subsistence farming. The objective of the proposed intervention is to improve food and income security of crisis affected people - including IDPs - in Bor South and Nyirol Counties of Jonglei State. The total number of people targeted is 52,183. The intervention would be integrated with an ongoing education project with the aim of building a safe and protective environment for children, which is currently receiving development support from Sida. This would foremostly be done by preventing dropout rates through cash assistance and livelihoods trainings, and by meeting nutritional needs of children under the age of five in order to prevent them from suffering physical or cognitive damages ahead of enrolling in school. The humanitarian project would be multisectoral - food security and livelihood, nutrition, child protection, mental health and psychosocial support, and with indirect links to education. The project would contribute to the three Strategic Objectives of the 2020 South Sudan HRP: reducing morbidity and mortality; facilitating safe, equitable and dignified access to basic services; and enabling vulnerable people to recover from crisis, seek solutions to displacement and build resilience to acute shocks and chronic stresses. Save the Children would partner with the local organization Christian Recovery and Development Agency (CRADA) in Nyirol for part of the food security and livelihood component, and cooperate with the Ministry of Agriculture, Ministry of Health, County Health Department, and Ministry of Gender. Syria - SEK 10,000,000 About to enter its tenth year, the war in Syria has devastated the country, forcing hundreds of thousands of people to live in overcrowded camps with insufficient services and imminent protection risks. In two of these camps located in northeast Syria - Al Hol and Roj - over 64,400 people live. In Al Hol, 94 % of the residents are women and children, and 53 % are below the age of 12. Around 60 % of children are not receiving education, with Covid-19 having further exacerbated this situation. In Roj, 64 % of the residents are below 18 years old, many similarly missing out on education opportunities. A barrier analysis conducted by Save the Children in mid-2020 indicated lacking access to services as a major concern, in particular for vulnerable groups such as girls and children with disabilities. The proposed intervention would address this issue through the provision of integrated protection, mental health, psychosocial, and education support reaching a targeted 1,700 children, 140 caregivers and 22 education facilitators. Activities include providing case management and psychosocial support services, making referrals, supporting child protection committees and promoting protective education opportunities. The intervention would contribute specifically to Strategic Objective 2 - enhance protection and Strategic Objective 3 - increase resilience and access to services, of the 2020 HRP for Syria, published in late 2020. Being one of few NGOs with access to operate in the camps, Save the Children would be conducting all implementation, while seeking to advocate with camp authorities on child-related issues and strengthen community structures such as child protection committees and parent teachers associations to promote resilience. Yemen - SEK 15,000,000 OCHA estimates that 24.1 million people are in need of humanitarian assistance (as of December 2020), which corresponds to around 80 % of the entire population. One of the governorates most severely affected by the war is Hajjah, with frontlines in Abs, Mustaba and Aslem where people suffer from severe deprivations and increased protection risks. In February 2019, for example, 62 % of cases of recruitment and use of children and 37 % of child casualties verified across the country were from Hajjah. In addition to the hostilities, displacement and lack of access are the main drivers of humanitarian needs, in particular food insecurity. Moreover, 5.5 million children were estimated to be in need of education assistance in 2020, with 161 schools in Hajjah unfit for use and girls being two times more likely th be withdrawn from school than boys. The proposed support is for an integrated food security and livelihoods, child protection and education intervention to 7,800 people (no double counting) in Abs district and Hajjah city. This will be done by, inter alia, providing multipurpose cash grants to adolescents and caregivers to cover basic needs, most of whom would also receive complementary vocational training with the aim to improve their livelihoods resilience. With regards to child protection, moreover, support services would complement education efforts by targeting children attending temporary learning spaces with psychosocial support and case management when needed. Save the Children's operations have previously suffered severely from restricted access - in 2019, merely 13 % of targeted beneficiaries for a Sida-funded project were reached in four northern provinces (including Hajjah), prompting Save the Children to shift its operations to southern Yemen in 2020. The outlook is currently that Save the Children would be able to conduct the intervention as planned for 2021, but Sida will need to engage in close dialogue with SCS during the year to ensure operations are running smoothly and that Sida is promptly informed otherwise. Finally, Ansar Allah, largely in control of north Yemen, has been subjected to a terrorist designation by the US as of 19 January 2021. Sida, Unit for Humanitarian Assistance is therefore in close contact with its partners on the potential impact of the designation on the humanitarian situation in the country, as well as the SCS’s specific activities and presence. Moreover, a risk analysis is being developed by each partner to identify challenges and mitigation measures. II. Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) - SEK 25,000,000 Part of the annual humanitarian budget is set aside for sudden onsets of humanitarian crises and as well as deteriorations of major ongoing ones. For these situations, Sida has a Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) that makes it possible to allow for the release of disbursed (but unallocated) funds for SPOs within 24 hours in order for them to swiftly respond when humanitarian needs suddenly emerge or severely deteriorate. SCS has been assessed by Sida to have a strong capacity to respond to sudden onset crises in complex humanitarian contexts. For this reason, it is proposed that SCS receives SEK 25 million in RRM support for 2021.
III. Capacity Building and Method Development Support Strengthening Humanitarian Access - SEK 3,409,000 As raised above, the latest Annual Report of the UN Secretary General on Children and Armed Conflict outlined an increase of 453 percent in incidents of denial of humanitarian access in 2019, representing a total of more than 4,400 incidents. In recent years, the respect for norms governing armed conflict and humanitarian action has eroded, which undermines the ability of humanitarian organizations to reach people in need of assistance and places the onus on communities themselves to ensure access to assistance and services. Moreover, access restrictions are sometimes further compounded by counterterrorism and sanction measures preventing engagement with actors that might be in partial or direct control over areas where humanitarian needs exist. The objective of this intervention is to address these issues by strengthening access for humanitarians and communities in hard-to-reach areas. It is divided along three objectives: 1. Promote systematization of how Save the Children staff and partners engage in dialogue with armed actors. This includes providing, inter alia, capacity-building support for field workers and frontline teams in structuring their humanitarian negotiations. 2. Facilitate communities to access services. 2021 would be the first year of a two-year effort to assemble knowledge and understanding and develop guidance to promote community-led child protection. The ambition is for this to then be piloted in selected constituencies during 2022 (no such funding for year two proposed for in this Appraisal Memo). 3. Measuring the impact of denial of humanitarian access to children, including the effects of counterterrorism legislation. This would be done as a research project in partnership with Watchlist and the Fordham University's Institute of International Humanitarian Affairs (IIHA) and be used for advocacy purposes. This proposed project aligns with several objectives of Sida's Humanitarian Strategy's, in particular "Humanitarian assistance and protection activities reach people in hard-to-reach areas" and "Humanitarian actors have safe, unhindered and sustained humanitarian access to reach crisis-affected people". Interagency Child Protection Programming - SEK 2,184,000 In a constantly evolving humanitarian landscape there is a need to ensure humanitarian actors respond to crises with quality and reach. To this effect, humanitarian standards are central instruments. Departing from this notion, the project aims to strengthen quality, accountability and efficiency in interagency child protection programming. It is based on two components: the Child Protection Minimum Standards (CPMS) and Cash and Voucher (CVA) assistance. First, together with the Sphere Protection Principles, the CPMS provide for a foundation of advancing Centrality of Protection in humanitarian programming, which was incorporated in the CPMS during 2019. However, funding for child protection is limited and prioritization of Centrality of Protection across sectors is oftentimes lacking. The proposed project seeks to address this by supporting innovation and local leadership through the CPMS Innovation Fund - granting financial support to national and local actors to lead implementation of the CPMS. Moreover, advocacy is planned for at the global level on how multi-sectoral actors' commitment to the Centrality of Protection can be realized and trickle down to programming at the country level. The second component seeks to strengthen the use and evidence base for CVA in interagency child protection programming, which in part is a continuation of activities funded by Sida in 2020. It includes (i) the finalization and dissemination of an integrated CVA and Child Protection Monitoring, Evaluation, Assessment and Learning (MEAL) toolkit, (ii) undertaking a desk review on CVA for child-headed households and unaccompanied children, and (iii) finalizing guidance on conditions and capacities required to work with child protection using CVA. This proposed project also aligns with several objectives of Sida's humanitarian Strategy's, including "Reduced risk of violence, threats and abuse for crisis-affected people", and "Increased effectiveness and efficiency of the humanitarian system in line with Grand Bargain commitments". IV. Global Surge Deployments - SEK 800,000 In 2017, a review was undertaken of the surge structure across the Save the Children movement, which resulted in a decision to transition it from a decentralized model where surge teams were hosted by different Members, to a centralized model hosted by SCI under what is called a Global Humanitarian Surge Platform (GHSP). The purpose was to increase the quality, speed and effectiveness of the global surge capacity, reducing the complexity of deployment procedures and increasing the visibility of supply and demand of staff. The GHSP was formally established in 2019, and managed 342 deployments in 2020. The objective of Sida's proposed support to the GHSP is to ensure that Save the Children's humanitarian responses have access to rapidly deployable skilled and experienced staff needed to deliver high quality and timely humanitarian responses. During 2021, an estimated ten deployments of four weeks respectively are expected to be funded through Sida's support. V. Operational and Technical Support - SEK 5 000 000 This support is provided to SCS's HQ in Stockholm in order to engender high-quality management of - and compliance with - the draft Agreement during 2021. The support is divided between "Operational Support", "Thematic and Quality Support", "Grants Management & Monitoring", and "Financial Management and Donor Relations". Sida's assessment of this support is provided in more detail in section 5.1. below.

description.narrative: Continued access to education in emergency affected counties of Jonglei state project, will deliver lifesaving education services to newly displaced IDPs and distressed children and youths who have sought refuge in Fangak County, and as well are those displaced within or into Uror County due to the fresh fights in Unity and upper Nile states. The proposed budget will support the provision of Psychosocial support services and life skills education for 5,230 school age boys and girls, ECD activities for 2,000 pre-school aged boys and girls and vocational training for 300 youths in selected population pockets of Nyalual, Toch, old fangak and Keew, in Fangak County of Jonglei state during the first half of 2016. Key messages on hygiene and health will contribute to the reduction in morbidities in among children, psychosocial support will relieve distress and restore normalcy, life skills will reduced the likelihoods for recruitment into armed groups, and vocational training will reduced the idleness among other associated tendencies i.e. recruitment and perpetuation of violence

description.narrative:
Urklipp från den sammanfattande resultatuppdatering 2022, exempel på resultat:
Samarbetet mellan olika aktörer inom teamen som också involverar en bredd av andra aktörer har visat på särskilt goda resultat.
Ett exempel som ges i den senaste årsrapporten är ett team i Etiopien där företrädare från Hälsoministeriet tillsammans med folkhälsovetare från icke-statliga organisationen Population Services International (PSI) samarbetat för att öka efterfrågan hos HIV-negativa kvinnor som säljer sex och tillgången till pre-expositionsprofylax mot HIV (PrEP) i enlighet med hälsoministeriets policy. De riktlinjerna och metoder som utvecklades av teamet har integrerats i Etiopiens nationella hiv/AIDS-program och medlemmarna från hälsoministeriet har bildat en Task Force inom ministeriet för att utvidga programmet på nationell nivå. Teamets förändringsinitiativ involverade förutom teamets hemorganisationer även vårdpersonal, läkemedelsföretag, lokala organisationer och peer-educators. En viktigt komponent var också att teamet kartlagt både formella och informella "gatekeepers" relevanta för HIV-preventivt arbete. Initiativet har hittills resulterat i att 90 procent av de 743 kvinnor som projektet nådde använde sig av PrEP efter 3 månader, vilket minskade till 77 procent efter 6 månader, troligtvis på grund av pandemin.
Ett annat exempel är i Bangladesh där en av deltagarna varit involverad och drivit inkluderandet av mental hälsa hos LGBTQ i "National Mental Health Strategic Plan 2020-2030" som ska godkännas av Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
I den senaste årsrapporten uppger mer än 80% av deltagarna att stöd från deras organisationer i att förankra förändringsinitiativen är avgörande för goda och hållbara resultat. Flera av teamen jobbar även för att förankra deras initiativ utanför den egna organisationer med andra relevanta aktörer som ministerier och FN-organ och därmed utvidga resultaten och öka hållbarheten.
Ett exempel är i Sudan där teamen presenterade sitt projekt för hälso- och utbildningsministerierna, UNFPA och UNESCO samt tidigare ITP-deltagare. Deltagarna arbetar på hälsoministeriet och samarbetade med Sudanese PLHV Care Association i Khartoum med 2000 medlemmar. Projektet syftar till peer-to-peer stöd bland människor som lever med HIV (PLHV) förbättra kunskap om SRHR inklusive preventivmedel bland PLHV.
Vad gäller organisatorisk förändring så rapporterar en majoritet av deltagarna att de infört nya arbetsrutiner och arbetsmetoder i deras organisationer och institutioner. Ett konkret exempel på nya arbetsrutiner är på ett sjukhus i Zimbabwe, där vissa arbetsuppgifter som tidigare enbart fick genomföras av läkare nu tagits över av barnmorskor och sjuksköterskor.
Hela 95 procent av deltagarna uppger i den senaste årsrapporten (014204/22) att de upplever en förbättrad attityd inom deras organisationer gentemot målgruppen, där ett gott och professionellt bemötande förväntas öka efterfrågan på SRHR-service. Ett exempel på detta finns på ett distriktssjukhus i Nairobi där efterfrågan på preventivmedel hos barn och ungdomar (10-24 år) ökat från 7 personer under en 6-månaders period till 95, som följd av ett förändringsprojekt lett av ett team från Pumwani Maternal Hospital för ökad kunskap och bemötande hos hälsopersonal. I hela disktriktet (Kamukunji sub-county) ökade efterfrågan med 16 procent under samma period. Teamet samarbetar med Ministry of Education och Ministry of Labour and Social Protection samt internationella organisationer som Röda korset, Hope Worldwide Kenya och DREAMS för att utöka initiativet.
Programmet bidrar även till forskning. Två tidigare ITP-deltagare har blivit doktorander vid Ethiopian Public Health Institute där de fokuserar på sexuellt våld. Vid Lunds universitet driver en doktorand ett forskningsprojekt för att studera lTP-SRHRs långsiktiga effekter, vilket resulterat i ett antal akademiska artiklar (dessa är författade tillsammans med genomförarna av programmet på LU). Dessa fokuserar just på attityder och bettenden bland hälsovårdspersonal i olika kontexter.
Insatsen har bidragit till flera liknande resultat i de olika deltagande länderna, dock syns ingen systematisk koppling mellan de olika förändringsinitiativen över tid och mellan programomgångar. Flera av initiativen i Kenya har haft ett fokus på preventivmedel och rådgivning bland ungdomar, men dessa har genomförts på olika lokala distrikt och sjukhus och det framgår inte i rapporteringen huruvida tidigare initiativ sammankopplats eller tagit del av senare. Denna sammankoppling försvåras också i och med att inte samma länder deltar i varje programomgång och att det därmed blir ett glapp mellan landsteamen. Under årsmötet diskuterades detta, och LU framförde att sammankopplingar görs, om än inte på ett systematiskt vis.
Samtidigt har flera initiativ breddats och utökats till ytterligare regioner än planerat, till exempel i Sydsudan där postpartum- och postabort- preventivmedelsrådgivning kunde ges till 1,658 kvinnor på tre olika sjukhus där sådan rådgivning inte erbjudits tidigare.

title.narrative: COVID-19 UN Women 2017-2021 Strategic Partnership Framework
COVID-19 UN Women 2017-2021 Strategic Partnership Framework

description.narrative: Reprogrammed funds to address COVID-19 Continuation of SPF, support to UNWomen´s Strategic Plan goal 1 and 4.

Omprogrammerade medel för att bekämpa covid-19 UN Women bildades 2010 genom beslut i FN:s generalförsamling och är operativt sedan den 1 januari 2011. UN Women arbetar med jämställdhet och kvinnors ökade egenmakt. UN Women har ett unikt mandat att leda, samordna och främja ansvarsutkrävande för hela FN-systemets arbete för jämställdhet och är sekretariat för FN:s Kvinnokommission (Commission on the Status of Women, CSW). Organisationen arbetar såväl normativt som operativt och ska ej ersätta övriga delar av FN-systemets jämställdhetsarbete. UN Womens målsättning är att uppmärksamma de jämställdhetsdimensioner som finns inom alla utvecklings- och MR-områden. Med utgångspunkt i den vision om jämställdhet som uttrycks i FN-stadgan arbetar UN Women bland annat för eliminering av diskriminering av kvinnor och flickor, kvinnors egenmakt och jämställdhet mellan kvinnor och män som mottagare av utveckling, MR, humanitär hjälp och fred och säkerhet. Organisationen arbetar även med att i samarbete med andra delar av FN-systemet formulera globala standarder och normer samt med att stödja medlemsländerna med implementering av dessa.
UN Women har ansökt till Sida om finansiering för "Strategic Partnership Framework 2017-2020" (SPF) med en total budget på 320 MSEK för fyra år.
Programmet är en fortsättning på det SPF som implementerades under 2011- 2016 med goda resultat. Resultaten bekräftas av en utvärdering av programmet samt en halvtidsöversyn av UN Womens strategiska plan 2014-2017. SPF 2017- 2020 syftar till att stödja UN Women att implementera sin Strategiska Plan 2014-2017 samt den nya Strategiska Planen som kommer att gälla 2018- 2021. Sidas finansiering kommer att gå till följande två resultatområden (Impact areas); 1) Öka kvinnors deltagande och inflytande i beslutsfattande organ; 4) Öka kvinnors ledarskap i fred, konflikt och humanitär respons. Programmet har en global ansats.
Sammanfattningsvis kommer det föreslagna programmet att bidra till: - Öka kvinnors ledarskap och deltagande, genom lagstiftning och policyer som förbättrar kvinnors rättigheter och genom att verka för kvinnors deltagande i beslutsfattande organ, samt genom att öka kvinnors politiska deltagande och inflytande.
- Öka kvinnors ledarskap i insatser för fred, säkerhet och humanitär respons genom att stärka implementeringen av kvinnor, fred och säkerhets åtaganden och ansvarsutkrävande ramverk i konflikt - och post konflikt länder, men även genom att stärka implementeringen av jämställdhetsåtaganden i humanitära insatser. Det bedöms relevant att humanitärt arbete omfattas av stödet då 80% av humanitära kriser sker i konfliktkontexter.
- Stärka UN Womens koordinering av FN systemet och dess partnerskap, resultatbaserade styrning, rapportering, kunskapshantering och utvärdering samt organisatorisk effektivitet på regional - och landnivå.

To deliver on its triple mandate, UN Women should lead issues on gender equality and the empowerment of women, and to promote accountability within the UN system (coordinating mandate), have universal coverage, strategic presence and provide support to intergovernmental policy and normative processes (normative mandate) and carry out programmes at country level (operational mandate).
The intervention will support two thematic areas of UN Women's Strategic Plan, Impact area 1: Increase women's leadership and participation and Impact area 4: to increase women's leadership in peace, security and humanitarian response.
The SPF has four intended outcomes (two per impact area).1.1 Legislation and policies to advance women's rights and promote their participation in decision-making bodies are reformed and adopted.1.2 Gender responsive measures (mechanisms, processes and services) promote women's leadership and participation in politics. 4.1 Women, Peace and Security commitments and accountability frameworks are adopted and implemented in conflict and post-conflict countries.4.2 Gender equality commitments adopted and implemented in humanitarian action which includes disaster risk reduction and preparedness, response and recovery.

description.narrative:
HIGHLIGHTS OF RESULTS FROM SPF II IN 2021:
SPF IIs outcomes are, since the inception, aligned with the outcomes of UN Womens Strategic Plan 2018-2021. The reporting shows, as previous years, that most indicators have surpassed their targets and it is evident that the program overall has progressed well and will reach most targets at the end of 2021.
UN Women does not report any unexpected results, but does mention the challenge that unexpected political developments and crises during 2021 posed to its planned implementation and expected results.
Apart from specifying a wide range of results within the two areas of WPP and WPS, the report, positively, includes a specific section on key partnerships during the year, as well as a section that highlights new developments, which UN Women sees as key. For example, the CSW65 Agreed Conclusions from 2021 which represent a historic normative advancement since the Member States reaffirm their commitment to women's political participation by setting the highest-ever international target for women's representation (50/50). The commitments urge governments and relevant stakeholders to leave no one behind in addressing the root causes of barriers to WPP by strengthening normative, legal, and regulatory frameworks, gender-responsive institutional reforms, and financing for WPP. UN Women's co-leadership in two pillars of the Secretary General's Call to Action for Human Rights (one on temporary special measures and one on elimination of discriminatory laws) is also mentioned here. Normative advances also included the enhanced focus on political and financial support to gender equality by the Gender Equality Forum in 2021, as a new Compact on WPS was launched and have received 160 signatories (Member states, civil society etc) for various commitments over a five year period. Sida takes note that the global furthering of the agenda is focused on implementation and not new resolutions or likewise. The new UN Women Humanitarian Strategy also marks an important new development.
Women's Political Participation, WPP
Overall: In the SPFII annual report of 2021, the results that relate to women's political participation are outlined within the main narrative report, as well as within the Annex C. Annex C provides an overview of the country-based programming supported by SPFII in 2021. Hence, although such results are covered within the main narrative report, Annex C provides a more detailed and in-depth picture of activities supported in 25 countries in Africa, Latin America and the Middle East. This is a larger number of examples presented than in the 2020 report (2020: 15 countries in the same three regions).
In summary, in 2021, UN Women provided in-country and remote policy guidance, and technical assistance, on WPP including expert deployments, to over 65 countries and six regional offices. Over USD 7,4 million in seed funding were provided to 40 countries and five regional offices. Consequently, legal and policy reforms were ensured, and enhanced WPP occurred in national and local elections in 26 countries. Over USD 200 million were, moreover, catalyzed for WPP programming. Sida sees it as positive that this figure is clearly monitored and presented within this year's report, since the reporting, historically, has merely presented the corresponding figure within the WPS area.
Outcome 1.1: Legislation and policies to advance women's rights and promote their participation in decision-making bodies are reformed and adopted.
Under this outcome, UN Women provides its UN Country Offices, as well as it national partners such as government agencies, electoral stakeholders, networks of women leaders, with technical assistance, as well as provides them with comparative knowledge and tools in order to ensure that policies and legislation, which promote womens political participation (WPP), are reformed, adopted and implemented. It is also under this outcome that UN Women provides its country offices with technical, financial (seed funds) and coordination support in order to ensure the same advances.
The CO offices in Iraq and Mexico are two examples of recipients of SPF seed funds in 2021. In Iraq, UN Women supported the Council of Ministers in Establishing a Supreme Committee (SC) with a mandate to promote women's participation and protection in Oct 2021 parliamentary elections. As the only UN agency nominated to sit on the SC (total 14 members, mostly government agencies), UN Women had a significant opportunity to provide assistance to the SC and its members. E.g. the Independent High Electoral Commission (IHEC), as one of the members, ensured a Electoral Code of Conduct with specific gender equality provisions, including provisions against VAWP. An important result was that all political parties in all governorates, the President, the Prime Minister and the Speaker of the Parliament all signed it. Additionally, that agency, together with the Department of Women's Empowerment (DWE), ensured the development of a training manual that was, subsequently, used by the IHEC and UN Women when they trained polling staff in a training-of-trainers approach that thereafter reached more than 6000 polling staff from all governorates, resulting in gender-responsive polling arrangements as per international standards concerning women's civil and political rights. In Mexico, ahead of their 2021 parliamentary elections, the seed funds to the CO were, for example, used to support the Electoral Institute of Oaxaca's innovative and culturally-sensitive communications campaign on preventing VAWP. The campaign included the production of guidance materials in indigenous languages and dissemination of such through social media and indigenous associated radio stations. Additionally, a specialised modular training was produced by the Local Electoral Institute, helping more than 180 indigenous and Afro Mexican female leaders and local public servants to enhance their capacities to engage in political life. Sida sees this as an important LNOB effort.
The reporting, furthermore, outlines a substantial number of knowledge products and tools that, in 2021, were developed, translated into different languages, and used, which offered UN Women's COs an important package of practical guidance and practice-informed research to support national programme implementation. E.g. a study on Effective, Decisive and Inclusive Women's Leadership in COVID-19 Response and Recovery (mapping lessons learned and recommendations), a Guidance Note on Preventing Violence Against Women in Politics (to COs and UNCTs on how to support Member States in addressing VAWP, including women HRDs, journalists, CSO activists), a Map on Women in Politics in 2021, etc. Also, importantly and for the first time, a comprehensive overview of women's political participation at the local level was provided within the working paper Women's Representation in Local Government: A Global Analysis by UN Women as the sole custodian agency for SDG indicator 5.5.1b. This is an important knowledge product as it aims to shift the global narrative from national to local decision-power, a less known but critical level of governance. A Women in Local Government website, an multi-year project, was also finalised and launched in 2021.
Harmonised data collection tools on VAWP, namely a series of questionnaires for officeholders, for political candidates, and for voters were developed, tested and implemented in 2021. These aim to fill a crucial knowledge gap in terms of measuring the magnitude of VAWP, identify the most frequent forms of and settings for such violence, what women are most a risk, who the main perpetrators are, what complaints mechanisms are used, etc. As a result of implementing these surveys, UN Women has generated the first ever comparable data on VAWP experienced by women, basically data on the aforementioned aspects, in five countries (Nepal, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine and Tunisia). Sida sees this as another crucial knowledge product and tool.
Last, but not least under this outcome, UN Women's SPF reporting also provides an account of the important contribution the programme has to strengthening its own staff capacities on WPP. It outlines that in response to the corporate thematic evaluation on WPP (2018) which called for increasing thematic capacity in the field, SPF funding has helped UN Women to ensure that COs have recruited national experts to fill gender knowledge gaps and increase capacity on WPP within various institutions such as electoral management bodies. It has also ensured that there are now regional WPP advisors in Europe, Central Asia, and in East and Southern Africa, but also that the existing thematic presence on WPP in Latin America, the Caribbean and the Arab States has been strengthened. UN Women outlines how beneficial this has been in terms of being able to ensure localised expertise as well as rapid responses to fluid political developments. It has also helped in building the capacity of aspiring women leaders and candidates, focusing on LNOB. Sida sees this as very positive and in line with its' expectations and hopes for the SPF. UN Women, furthermore, outlines that having these regional advisers and thematic policy and programme staff, as well as flexible resources, has given UN Women the necessary institutional capacity to have a seat at the table when it matters the most, and to be able to respond to country-level requests with active support and guidance, even where UN Women is a non-resident agency.
Outcome 2.1: Gender responsive measures (mechanisms, processes and services) promote women's leadership and participation in politics.
Under this outcome, UN Women provides technical assistance, knowledge-sharing and capacity strengthening to parliaments, executive cabinets, and local legislatures to promote gender equality and womens empowerment. Moreover, womens political participation as candidates, voters, and elected leaders is strengthened, as well as womens leadership more generally, through capacity strengthening.
UN Women reports that 20 country offices have supported parliaments, ministerial cabinets and local legislatures to pass legislation and measures that promote gender equality. Parliamentary discussions on new laws on VAWP passed in Brazil and El Salvador, involving parliamentary women's caucuses and CSOs, were assisted.
Through SPF support over 3000 women leaders, aspiring candidates and elected officials in 19 countries enhanced their political leadership and networking skills in campaign planning, communications and messaging, constituency outreach and networking during 2021. More countries but less individuals were covered this year in comparison with last year (2020: more than 4000 individuals in ten countries). Specific examples and results are highlighted from Kyrgyzstan, Nigeria, Zimbabwe and Bolivia. The latter being the virtual training programme on Women's Political Rights and Young Leadership delivered to 259 young members of Municipal Youth Councils, designed and implemented by UN Women Bolivia together with the Vice Ministry of Equal Opportunities and the Plurinational School of Public Management (EGPP), which Sida visited during its field trip in March/April 2022. The training provided the young women with knowledge and tools to support their active role as promoters of peaceful political dialogue and agents of change for gender equality in their communities.
Important examples of results in terms of gender sensitive reforms adopted by political institutions, UN Women reports about the establishment of a National Observatory of Women in Politics in Brazil. The multi-stakeholder mechanism aims to investigate, monitor and centralise research on women's political representation at federal, state and municipal levels. Moreover, in Bolivia, 48 municipalities out of 137 targeted modified their internal regulations so that they reflect VAWP after having received training and technical assistance on Bolivia's law against harassment and violence against women in politics. In Jordan, the Royal Committee to Modernize the Political System has produced recommendations that include a new elections law (introducing Temporary Special Measures, TSMs), a new political parties law and related constitutional recommendations, as well as specific recommendations on how to improve local administration for women and youth's effective engagement in public life. Consultations on these recommendations provided a platform for dialogue with a wide range of stakeholders and raised awareness about the recommendations. UN Women also supported the Ministry of Political and Parliamentary Affairs (MOPPA) to organise a workshop with women parliamentarians and senators to discuss the recommendations which allowed the MPs to directly discuss these recommendations with the Minister and and the the members of the Royal Committee.
Outcome 3.1: Constitutions and legal frameworks to advance gender equality and women's rights are reformed and adopted.
Under this outcome, UN Women works to support constitutional and legal reforms. SPF continued to engage with field offices and UN partners to support the development and implementation of gender responsive legal frameworks and it continued to enable UN-Women to advance on the implementation of the Equality in Law for Women and Girls by 2030: A Multi-stakeholder Strategy for Accelerated Action.
Specifically in 2021, the SPF, through policy guidance, technical assistance and seed funding, contributed to the initiation of legislative reviews in Cote d'Ivore, Burundi, Central African Republic, Haiti, Mozambique and Zimbabwe. Also, a comprehensive legislative review was undertaken in five Caribbean countries: Trinidad and Tobago, the Bahamas, Barbados, Belize and Guyana. The aim of the reviews is to determine how the constitution, statutes, laws, administrative regulations, etc., specifically relating to women and girls, impact on the achievement of gender equality.
During the SPFII, UN Women provided seed funding to 19 countries that directly contributed to successful programming within legal and justice reform processes. Examples of seed fund results in 2021 include supporting UN Women's joint UN work with the Constitutional Convention (in charge of drafting the new constitution) in Chile aiming to mainstream gender in the constitutional reform, as well as supporting Egypt's National Council for Women's (NCW's) discussions with MPs leading up to the tabling of procedural revisions of the law that governs personal status affairs (which governs marriage, divorce, inheritance, child custody, etc.). In the latter case, several knowledge products were generated and the NCW has developed initial procedural revisions of the Family Law that will be submitted to the Cabinet in 2022. In Nigeria UN Women CO carried out of review of the constitution from a gender perspective, identifying numerous proposed changes that promote women's rights, and in Tanzania, the CO supported the Tanzania Women Judges Association (TAWJA) in designing a Gender Bench Book on Women's Rights that aims to ensure that the capacity of the judiciary to ascertain women's access to justice is strengthened. A directive was subsequently issued by the Minister of Constitution and Legal Affairs to the Judiciary to further use the book to strengthen prosecutors' and state attorney's capacity to handle cases in gender sensitive ways, especially cases that affect women and girls left behind like rights of persons with disabilities, those living with HIV/AIDS, young and elderly women.
Women, Peace and Security
Overall: In this part of the report some results and changes for the WPS agenda at large, and on a global longer term in relation to the Security Council is accounted and analysed in Annex B, in addition to the outcome and output based progress report. The in-depth piece includes a focus on occurred changes and the the role of UN Women and, to the extent possible, the SPF modality and strategic partnership. Furthermore, Annex D contains a brief on WPS and disability inclusion (as part of the Leave No One Behind approach) and gives a broader stock taking, despite not being SPF specific.
As previous years, the report under this outcome suggests a high degree of synergistic funding, where SPF has served as a catalytic instance to attract other funding mechanisms, and thus, contributed to a strong increase in overall WPS funding. The programme overall encompasses activities and deployments in 49 countries, five regional offices and expertise to five investigation missions.
Also during 2021, Covid-19 continued to take its toll, and paired with complex political and security challenges in many countries, this jointly hampered and even reversed impact of certain interventions during the period.
Outcome 4.1 Women, Peace and Security commitments and accountability frameworks are adopted and implemented in conflict and post-conflict countries
Under this outcome, a large part of the funding is designated for staff capacities as a method to enhance UN Women's WPS capacities at all levels, and in 2021 this translated into 28 long-term experts and 12 short-term, an increase from 2020 (22 and 9 respectively).
One key area of work is for UN Women to support countries production, adoption and implementation (also localization) of National Action Plans (NAP) on WPS. It is reported that to date, 103 countries have now adopted a National Action Plan on WPS, compared to the 37 which were in place when the first phase of SPF started. This work includes for example technical assistance, in-put on drafts, arrangement of consultations, trainings, gatherings of best practise and political advocacy. 12 countries adopted new plans in 2021, four of whom processed their first plan and received assistance from UN Women to do so, e.g. Malawi, Mexico, Peru and UAE and six countries who have processed but not yet adopted NAPs (Chad, Ethiopia, Libya, Tajikistan, Uruguay and Vietnam). The work on enhancing implementation of NAPs is also reported for a large number of countries (24) and localization efforts in an increasing number of countries, including for 2021 DRC, Kyrgyzstan, Iraq, Philippines, Sudan and Ukraine.
UN Women's work with NAPs was part of the corporate evaluation finalised in 2020, but disseminated in 2021, leading to stronger focus on supporting the implementation of plans instead of creating new ones. Below are some more specific samples of results and achievements:
Some high end results are reported as being part of the NAP processes, like the DRC government commitment to a 30 per cent quota for women in decision making bodies, or in Jordan, where the armed forces and the public security directorate adopted a first ever gender mainstreaming strategy which included the appointment of 77 gender advisers and focal points and six gender champions. Increased targets has been set for higher female representation in peace keeping, and a first all-female police unit was deployed to the UN mission in DRC.
The efforts to "localize" NAPs have in 2021 been the continued focus in the Philippines, Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao, resulting in 20 provincial government actions plans where women's involvement was strengthened in the work with security actors and former combatants. Also in DRC and Ukraine have the support to localized plans been reported a priority - the former including a SPF-funded expert deployed to the Eastern parts of the country in order to support a provincial NAP in Ituri, and the latter leading to eleven adopted local action plans in, the then, conflicts affected regions of Luhansk, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. As part of the set-up of a secretariat at steering committee for Niger, this resulted not only in a more whole-of government approach but also in operational and financial plans for all the regions in the country. In Iraq the process of a monitoring plan of NAP resulted in sectorial plans for all ministries and a specific plan for Kurdistan. And despite Mexico having its first NAP, the progress reported in terms of net work building of women peace builders have already resulted in integration in 11 states and 54 municipalities.
In other countries, like Armenia and Azerbaijan, the conflict dynamics between the countries in Nagorno-Karabakh have influenced amendment and review of respective NAP processes and UN Women reports that its support has been amended accordingly for stronger influence on gender integration in overall responses to the conflict.
It is important to take note of how sudden changes in conflicts alters the prerequisites, or lead to back lash and even reverse results, like in the case of Myanmar, a country which had very good implementation levels of its localization process in Mon and Kayin states before the military take over. But after February 2021, these processes had to be put on hold as women's organisations had to leave the country, offices were raided and staff detained and abilities to participate in any political conversations disappeared. Furthermore, military control of financial resources increased risks for both UN Women and its partners. The same dynamics is reported for the localization of NAPs in Blue Nile ad South Darfur in Sudan, after the military coup.
Another part of the work under this outcome relates to the global normative frame works and to strengthen global commitments. In this line, SPF continued to fund and serve as the secretariat for the WPS Focal Point network with its 91 members. The network enables a close coordination among Member States and create a space to periodically share and exchange lessons learned and best practices. In 2021 focus has particularly been on the enhancement of the knowledge hub. An important task for SPF globally has been to launch and serve the new WPSHA compact which was launched at the Generation Equality forum in 2021 and now has 160 signatories. The compact is set out as a voluntary mechanism to enhance for example coordination, implementation, monitoring and accountability of WPS commitments. SPF also continued to fund the secretariat function of the Informal Experts Group which is directly connected to the Security Council.
From the reporting (Annex B) an internal assessment elaborates on the changes in the Security Council and the impact the SPF has played for supporting progress over time. It constitutes an excellent example of how allowing a more analytical approach to the SPF, changes, transformation and real results can be elaborated and the reporting can move away from activity based reporting. This annex spells out what the SPF has contributed to, for example by serving as the secretariat to the Security Councils informal experts group on WPS, which has steeply improved the councils knowledge and deliberations. In addition, the SPF has enabled UN Women to engage with the SC with briefs, monthly meetings with council members, UN and civil society, participation of female briefer, collaborations, follow-up, advising and facilitating advocacy opportunities, including contribution to the NGO Working Group (receiving support directly from Swedish MFA). These measures jointly can be seen to a larger or lesser direct degree having influenced council decisions and its deliberations over the past ten years. Just a few numbered examples:
- Two thirds of SC resolutions have WPS language (compared to one third in 2010) and the quality, areas and details have improved a lot. In general, the tilt towards only having CRSV language has balanced out and includes the rest of the agenda like participation and leadership.
- Female briefers to the SC has increased immensely. Between 2000-2015 there were 25 in all, compared to 2021 when that reached 60 women. Before 2016 no women was ever invited to specific country specific meetings, which is now a routine practise and happens several times every month.
The short-term experts, which were deployed to investigate sexual and gender based violence, the level of documentation and evidence collection in line with international standards increased in Belarus, Ethiopia, Libya, South Sudan and Syria. It is noteworthy that the SPF-funding has been used as a "gap-filler" for these kind of tasks - and over the years the amount of experts used have been dependent on other funding sources. This could under other circumstances be perceived as a weakness, while in the case of SPF this is welcomed as Sida want this funding mechanism to work flexibly in favour of UN Women being able to fulfill all its mandates under the chosen thematic areas. In Belarus it has, for example, led to an revelation of how systematic SGBV has been used as torture against both women and men in detention, especially as punishment against protesters, pro-opposition and also with a specifics target to LGBTIQ (perceived) individuals. In the Tigray region in Ethiopia it could be proved that all parties to the conflict committed SGBV to the level of war crimes and crimes against humanity, and these findings now serve the new international commission of Inquiry.
In this section there are numerous examples of synergistic funding being mobilised out of SPF funded staff, both in terms of other donors but also when applying and pushing other funds and mechanisms (like the WPHF, PBF, MPTF:s etc) to increase gender commitments. Regionally, it is reported that the advisers often have key roles in these processes. In Latin America and the Caribbean the adviser has mobilised 9,5 M USD in 2021 and with a further 3 M USD to be confirmed, as she helped and professionalized processes for a large number of offices. And in West and Central Africa she contributed to 3 M USD in new resources and 10 M USD awaiting. At times the regional advisers also strengthens the national offices for certain tasks, like in Chad. But also other SPF funded specialists have supported funding proposals, for example in CAR, DRC and Ethiopia.
In some countries, where UN Women has a long-term and strong collaboration and partnerships on WPS, the results are oftentimes broad in scope and expands to a large variety and cross-cutting areas. An example is Lebanon where results are reported for greater gender parity in the armed forces as well as broad mobilization on quotas for political participation, advancement of NAPs etc. Also Colombia showcase a strong WPS portfolio, strategic collaborations and influence in central processes like the Truth Commission and UN Verification team, as well as monitoring of gender provisions of the peace agreement, grants for protection of women human rights defenders etc.
There are a few other examples in the report of SPF being instrumental when it comes to women's direct participation in peace related processes, like for pushing the women 35 per cent quotas in South Sudan Revitalized Peace Agreement, leading to actual women's representation increase at community levels despite in modest terms. Support was also given to women's participation in track 2 processes between government and SPLM in Sudan, bringing together various fractions of the latter to agree on WPS priorities later presented in the Juba negotiations.
Humanitarian Action and Disaster Risk Reduction
Overall: The progress report outlines a lot of results and is, furthermore, complemented by Annex C which have short summaries of country specific work.
Outcome 4.2 Gender equality commitments adopted and implemented in humanitarian action which includes disaster risk reduction and preparedness, response and recovery
Under this outcome the SPF funded short- and long term deployments of experts are contributing to integrating gender into humanitarian action and its various frame works, providing inter-agency training/capacity building, technical expertise, as well as activating some seed funding for project implementation. In 2021 this meant disbursing gender expertise to 87 per cent of the humanitarian cluster system (where UN Women is present) and refugee responses in over 40 country and regional contexts. UN Women also serves as an accountability and monitoring mechanism for gender commitments in humanitarian actions, partly as part of the Inter-Agency Standing Committee, IASC, set-up.
The report contains numerous accounts of instances where UN Women are active members and have the ambition to influence, like Humanitarian Country Teams (or its equivalent) and lead, or as co-lead, Gender in Humanitarian Action Working Group, and in Regional and Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction, DRR. As mentioned above, UN Women, reports on its continued work with the IASC Gender Accountability Framework report which is providing analysis on the compliance with IASC policy set gender commitments, standards and roles and responsibilities of 31 UN coordinated humanitarian response planning cycles. To this end, UN Women refers to outcomes which involves collaboration with other UN agencies, notably UNHCR, UNFPA and UN OCHA. As examples: a global MoU has been signed with UNHCR; the collaboration with UN OCHA (and IFRC) deepened in terms of promoting and normatively influence women's leadership in humanitarian settings; and a joint global partnership with UNFPA was initiated, resulting in a CERF global grant to UN-Women in November 2020 in six countries with a focus on GBV, both survivors and at risk populations.
Localization of the agenda has been an important approach and, for example, under the Grand Bargain frame work, UN Women produced three guidance notes on gender responsive localization, participation revolution and harmonized needs assessments. The guidance note on localization has been adopted by IASC.
Due to restrictions on travel, and in order to be cost-effective, UN Women refers to a new launch of a seven week training materials being converted into digital platforms - where access to gender in humanitarian program cycle can be increased.
Under the work of Disaster Risk Reduction and Resilience numerous results are reported, especially along the normative and coordination mandates where women's agency in these processes are at the core. As reported last year, gender was mainstreamed into the UN Plan of Action on Disaster Risk Reduction for Resilience 2015-2030 progress review. This led to a study and recommendations for the advancement of womens agency and leadership in disaster risk reduction. This has since informed the whole UN Plan of Action which is now to be monitored. During 2021 it is reported that UN Women has provided technical support to preparatory processes for the regional and global platforms for DRR, thus strategically advancing gender equality in this regard. At a high end, this resulted in the SG including a focus on closing the gender gap in DRR in the report on the implementation of the Sendai framework 2015-2030. Also, it is reported that the SPF funded DRR specialist supported the CEDAW General Recommendation (No 37) on gender related DRR in relation to climate change. At regional level this included the gender-responsive European Forum for DRR Roadmap (2021-2030) and Caribbean Regional Action plan.
Various materials and tools have been developed when it comes to gender-responsive DRR and resilience, in all cases in collaboration with other agencies like the World Bank, Unicef, EU and UNDRR. Synergistic funding between SPF and Australia has resulted in a Women's Resilience to Disasters Knowledge Hub, including a tracker of progress.
SPF funds continued to be used in order to build up a Women's Resilience to Disasters Programme and Humanitarian action in 2021. The approach has attracted other donors and its aim is to enhance womens agency and leadership for humanitarian response and disaster resilience in order to challenge gender-responsive norms, policies, strategies, systems, mechanisms and tools and standards globally. When it comes to building evidence and accountability, particular country examples are raised for the Asia and Pacific region as well as Vietnam, South Sudan, Haiti and Mexico, showcasing a broad samples of development of tool kits, analysis, studies, recommendations, forums and follow-up - mainly in line with the normative mandate at regional or national levels and often with a nexus approach and oftentimes as a collaboration with governments.
To enhance national and regional capacities, UN-Women provided dedicated gender expertise and technical assistance to Humanitarian Country Team members, particularly UN OCHA and the health cluster, on gender and humanitarian action, gender data, and to create an evidence base.
There are various examples provided, including the case of the refugee camp Cox´s Bazar in Bangladesh (where SPF funds the Head of office) where a broad strategic collaboration with the police, civil society, humanitarian actors and women's organisations has resulted in reinforced gender mainstreaming and women and girls in site management. In most reported cases UN Women provided capacity development or technical assistance of key partners (Asia Pacific, Fiji, Kiribati, Samoa, Tonga, Vanuatu, Solomon Islands, Myanmar, Nepal) often to the end of gender mainstreaming, developing tools, action plans etc. In some country settings, like the example of Lebanon, real time gender data was used to influence the humanitarian response not only nationally but also at regional and global levels, which is reported to have changed several policy decisions. In Palestine this work has led to an evidently stronger integration (and positioning in OCHA) of gender i humanitarian action. UN Women is working in partnerships and in Jordan, for example, to enhance a survivor centered approach to GBV, taking root in legislation and protection.
Organisational Effectiveness and Efficiency
UN Women reports that the findings of SPFIIs Mid-Term Review (MTR) have been fully addressed with 15 of the 17 key actions adopted in response have been completed, another 2 are no longer applicable. A direct result of the recommendations is, for example, the impact assessments of WPS and the Security Council. Sida sees this as positive given that all findings, by the closure of the activity period for this contribution, are handled.
Delivery in terms of finance and programmatic targets has been high since the inception of SPF and has increased, despite a dip due to Covid-19 in 2020.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published

title.narrative: Provision of Emergency Robust Shelter to Vulnerable Displaced and Displacement Affected Population in Melut County

description.narrative: In the past few Years, DRC using UNHCR grants, provided targeted emergency shelters assistance and access to basic services for persons with specific needs (PWSNs) and their families, through the provision of acute emergency shelters kits made of plastic sheets, small bamboo sticks and few nails. The continuation of conflict, protracted displacement and additional influxes into displacement sites in Melut County (Dethoma 1 amp 2, Korhadar, Malek and New Paloich School) are expected to continue in through 2017. Providing shelters being a process rather than a product, this project aims to ensure the continued provision of essential emergency Shelters services to vulnerable displaced population in different sites within Melut County, through the implementation of construction in line with the Shelter/NFI Cluster objectives, humanitarian best practices and protection and gender considerations. DRC will run a shelter assessment in different IDPs sites in Melut County to identify vulnerable households eligible to benefit an upgrade to a robust emergency shelter which enhance the living conditions of 2400 individuals by providing them with more dignified shelter solution. The provision of the robust emergency shelters includes shelter construction assistance. 5 % of the beneficiaries will come from the hosts communities. This new shelter solution is designed through a beneficiary participated process, by giving beneficiaries a chance to choose the model they would like and recommending minor adjustments which can be accommodated in the budget limits. Although beneficiaries of the robust emergency shelter stage are well targeted, the projects also aim for a long-term impact of enhancing communities through improving local construction techniques. Therefore DRC will ensure that beneficiaries and their communities are involved during the whole project implementation period, starting from the design phase. In order to select beneficiaries following the set vulnerability criteria, forecast the shelters needs and to inform the shelter programming, DRC shelter team will conduct shelter assessments on several sites in Melut County, security permitting, and will conduct surveys on intentions, following age and gender dis-aggregation. All DRC shelter programme activities are conducted jointly with DRC camp management and protection units to ensure basic protection concerns considering age and sex are captured and future programming anticipated.
